citations.quote: Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. If Omega has the specified finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, then $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F=\sum_j\int_{S_j}F\cdot\nu_j\,dS$, with faces counted once off E. All integrals are finite. In a specified finite gluing, the two fluxes on every shared face cancel.

Let a finite gluing of elementary solid regions be given, with union $E$ and outer boundary presentation $\Sigma^{\mathrm{out}}=\bigl((D_1,\varphi_1),\ldots,(D_M,\varphi_M)\bigr)$. Vector-valued integrals below are taken coordinatewise, so that for a continuous $\mathbb R^3$-valued $W$ on $E$ the symbol $\iiint_EW$ denotes the vector whose $k$th coordinate is $\int_EW_k$, and for a continuous $\mathbb R^3$-valued $Z$ on the boundary the symbol $\iint_{\partial E}Z$ denotes the vector whose $k$th coordinate is $\sum_{j=1}^M\int_{D_j}Z_k(\varphi_j)$, where $n$ inside such an integrand is read as the oriented area vector $\varphi_{j,u}\times\varphi_{j,v}$ of the patch, exactly as in the scalar flux.

Then, for $f$ of class $C^1$ on an open set containing $E$ and $F$ of class $C^1$ on an open set containing $E$,

$$\iiint_E\nabla f=\iint_{\partial E}fn,\qquad \iiint_E\operatorname{curl}F=\iint_{\partial E}n\times F.$$

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p<\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then the compactly supported smooth
functions $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ are dense in
$W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$: for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ with
$$\|\varphi-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)}<\delta.$$
No such norm-density assertion is made for $p=\infty$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume countable choice. For every measure space and $1\le p\le\infty$, $L^p(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is complete. Every sequence converging in this norm has a subsequence of measurable representatives converging a.e. to a measurable representative of its norm limit. For finite $p$ no pointwise convergence of the whole sequence is asserted.

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

- For $0<p<\infty$, define an equivalence relation on $\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ by
  $$f\sim g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f-g\in\mathcal N(\mu),$$
  and write $L^p(\mu)$ for the set of classes $[f]$.
- For $p=\infty$, define the same relation on $L^\infty(\mu)$ and again write
  $L^\infty(\mu)$ for the set of classes.

Thus an element of $L^p(\mu)$ is an almost-everywhere equivalence class of
measurable representatives.

When $1\le p\le\infty$, the displayed set quotient agrees with the usual
quotient-vector-space construction of
[[def-quotient-vector-space-and-canonical-projection]].

For $0<p<1$, the same class notation is used; under its stated choice hypothesis, the later item
[[thm-the-l-p-distance-for-zero-less-p-less-one-is-a-complete-translation-invariant-metric]]
supplies the metric structure rather than a normed-space structure.

For $n\ge1$, there exists $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$, $\chi=1$ on $|x|\le1$, and $\chi=0$ on $|x|\ge2$. For $R>0$, $\chi_R(x)=\chi(x/R)$ satisfies $\partial^\beta\chi_R(x)=R^{-|\beta|}(\partial^\beta\chi)(x/R)$. The construction requires no choice.

derivations.claim: [The divergence of the radial weight] On $\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ one has $\operatorname{div}(x/|x|^2)=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_i(x_i|x|^{-2})=3|x|^{-2}-2|x|^{-2}=|x|^{-2}$, because the derivative of $|x|^{-2}$ in the direction $x$ is $-2|x|^{-4}\sum_ix_i^2=-2|x|^{-2}$.

[Integration by parts on the punctured space] Let $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\};\mathbb C)$ and put $W(x):=|u(x)|^2x/|x|^2$. Then $W$ is $C^1$ on $\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ and compactly supported there, and step 1.1 gives $\operatorname{div}W=
abla(|u|^2)\cdot x/|x|^2+|u|^2/|x|^2$. Since $\int_{\mathbb R^3}\operatorname{div}W=0$ by [F1], and $
abla(|u|^2)=2\operatorname{Re}(\overline u\,
abla u)$, we obtain $\int_{\mathbb R^3}|u|^2/|x|^2\,dx=-2\operatorname{Re}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\overline u(x)\,x\cdot
abla u(x)\,|x|^{-2}\,dx$.

[Hardy bound away from the origin] With $u$ as in step 2.1, the absolute value of the right-hand integral is at most $\int(|u|/|x|)|
abla u|\le\|u/|\cdot|\|_2\|
abla u\|_2$ by [F2], while the left-hand side is $\|u/|\cdot|\|_2^2$; both quantities are finite by [F6]. Hence $\|u/|\cdot|\|_2^2\le2\|u/|\cdot|\|_2\|
abla u\|_2$, and if the factor is zero the conclusion is immediate, and otherwise division by its positive value yields $\|u/|\cdot|\|_2\le2\|
abla u\|_2$, which is (a).

[Removing the puncture] Let $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ and use the radial $\chi=1-\chi_0\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3;[0,1])$ of [F7], with $\chi=0$ for $|x|\le1$, $\chi=1$ for $|x|\ge2$ and $|
abla\chi|\le C$; put $\chi_\varepsilon(x):=\chi(x/\varepsilon)$. Then $u_\varepsilon:=\chi_\varepsilon u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\};\mathbb C)$, because its support is contained in the closed set $\{|x|\ge\varepsilon\}\cap\operatorname{supp}u$ and hence stays a positive distance from the origin, so step 3.1 applies: $\|u_\varepsilon/|\cdot|\|_2\le2\|
abla u_\varepsilon\|_2$. As $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ the functions $u_\varepsilon/|x|$ converge to $u/|x|$ pointwise on $\{|x|>0\}$ and are dominated by $|u|/|x|\in L^2$ by [F6], so $\|u_\varepsilon/|\cdot|\|_2	o\|u/|\cdot|\|_2$ by [F5] applied to the squared moduli. Moreover $
abla u_\varepsilon=\chi_\varepsilon
abla u+u
abla\chi_\varepsilon$ with $\|\chi_\varepsilon
abla u-
abla u\|_2^2\le\int_{|x|<2\varepsilon}|
abla u|^2	o0$ and, with $M:=\|u\|_\infty$, $\|u
abla\chi_\varepsilon\|_2^2\le C^2\varepsilon^{-2}\int_{|x|\le2\varepsilon}M^2\,dx\le C^2M^2	frac{4\pi(2\varepsilon)^3}{3\varepsilon^2}=O(\varepsilon)	o0$; hence $\|
abla u_\varepsilon\|_2	o\|
abla u\|_2$, and passing to the limit in the display gives (b).

[Density extension to $W^{1,2}$] Let $u\in W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ and choose $u_n\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ with $\|u_n-u\|_{W^{1,2}}	o0$ by [F3]. Step 4.1 applied to $u_n-u_m$ gives $\|u_n/|\cdot|-u_m/|\cdot|\|_2\le2\|
abla(u_n-u_m)\|_2$, so $(u_n/|\cdot|)$ is Cauchy in $L^2$; let $w\in L^2$ be its limit, so $\|w\|_2\le2\|
abla u\|_2$ because $\|
abla u_n\|_2	o\|
abla u\|_2$. By [F4] some subsequence satisfies $u_{n_k}	o u$ and $u_{n_k}/|\cdot|	o w$ pointwise a.e.; on the conull set where $u_{n_k}	o u$ and $|x|>0$ we have $u_{n_k}(x)/|x|	o u(x)/|x|$, so $w=u/|\cdot|$ a.e. and (c) follows.

boundaries.reason: The lemma quantifies over a single function u; it contains no family, sum or intersection that could be empty.

boundaries.evidence: The zero function is allowed: both sides of the inequality read 0 for u=0, and the identity of step 2.1, div W = |u|^2/|x|^2, vanishes identically there.

boundaries.reason: No case at the value 1 occurs: the statement fixes dimension 3 and the constant 4, and no normalization of u is imposed.
The lemma has no multiplicity or degeneracy notion; the sharp constant 4 is not claimed to be attained.

boundaries.evidence: The punctured origin is the boundary of the test class (a): step 2.1 integrates by parts on R^3 minus the origin, and step 4.1 removes the puncture with the cutoff chi_eps, whose gradient bound |grad chi| <= C/eps is exactly what the epsilon -> 0 estimate needs.
The statement assumes Countable Choice; step 4.1 selects a sequence of cutoffs chi_{1/k} (countable, deterministic) to exhaust the punctured class, which is the only choice-like step.

boundaries.reason: The lemma is a one-directional inequality with a density corollary (c), not a biconditional.
No converse is stated: the lemma explicitly declines any claim about u outside W^{1,2}.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), let $d\ge1$ and work on $H=L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ ([[def-hilbert-space]]).

(a) For a real measurable finite-valued function $a:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ define $M_af:=af$ on $D(M_a):=\{f\in H: af\in H\}$. Then $M_a$ is a densely defined self-adjoint operator on $H$ ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]).

(b) Let $c>0$, $b\in\mathbb R$, and let $\mathcal F_2$ be the unitary Plancherel transform with the convention $\widehat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}dx$ on $L^1$ ([[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]], [[thm-plancherel]]). Define

$$H_0:=\mathcal F_2^*\,M_{c|\xi|^2+b}\,\mathcal F_2,\qquad D(H_0):=\{f\in H:|\xi|^2\mathcal F_2f\in H\}.$$

Then $H_0$ is self-adjoint, $D(H_0)$ coincides with the Sobolev space $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ as a set (with equivalent norms, [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[thm-fourier-characterisation-of-integer-order-hilbert-sobolev-spaces]]), $H_0\ge b$ in the quadratic-form sense, and for every Schwartz function $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, $H_0f=-(c/4\pi^2)\Delta f+bf$.

(c) If $V:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ is measurable with $\|V\|_\infty<\infty$ and $H:=H_0+M_V$ with domain $D(H_0)$, then $H$ is self-adjoint on $D(H_0)$, is bounded below, and the assignment $t\mapsto e^{itH}$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group whose generator is $iH$: the limit $\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t(e^{itH}\psi-\psi)$ exists exactly for $\psi\in D(H)$ and equals $iH\psi$ ([[lem-self-adjoint-operator-generates-a-strongly-continuous-unitary-group]]).

(d) *Scope*: the argument uses only boundedness and measurability of $V$; it proves nothing for $V\propto-1/|x|$, $V\propto|x|^2$ or the delta interaction, does not identify $H_0$ with any measured free-particle Hamiltonian, and asserts no physical interpretation.

Assume Countable Choice, let $n\ge1$ and $k\in\mathbb N_0$, and use complex
scalars. Write $W^{k,2}=W^{k,2}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ for the weak-derivative
Sobolev space of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], whose classes carry
the weak derivatives $D^\alpha f\in L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ for
$|\alpha|\le k$ and the norm
$$\|f\|_{W^{k,2}}=\Bigl(\sum_{|\alpha|\le k}\|D^\alpha f\|_2^2\Bigr)^{1/2},$$
and let $H^k=H^k(\mathbb R^n)$ be the real-order Bessel-potential completion
of [[def-real-order-bessel-potential-sobolev-space]] with its canonical
embedding $E_k:H^k\to\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$
([[thm-bessel-potential-completions-embed-in-tempered-distributions]]). Let
$u_f\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ denote the regular tempered distribution of
an $L^2$ class $f$. Then:

1. $E_k[H^k]=\{u_f:f\in W^{k,2}\}$, and
   $\Phi(f):=E_k^{-1}(u_f)$ is a bijection
   $\Phi:W^{k,2}\to H^k$. Thus, under the regular-distribution embedding,
   $W^{k,2}$ and $H^k$ are the same subspace of $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$.
2. There are constants $0<c_k\le C_k<\infty$, depending only on $n$ and $k$,
   with
$$c_k^{1/2}\,\|\langle\xi\rangle^k\mathcal F_2f\|_2\le\|f\|_{W^{k,2}} \le C_k^{1/2}\,\|\langle\xi\rangle^k\mathcal F_2f\|_2,$$
   and $\|\langle\xi\rangle^k\mathcal F_2f\|_2=\|\Phi(f)\|_{H^k}$. Hence the
   weak-derivative norm and the bracket-weighted $L^2$ norm are equivalent,
   and the latter is also equivalent to
   $\|(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{k/2}\mathcal F_2f\|_2$, by
$$\|\langle\xi\rangle^k h\|_2\le\|(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{k/2}h\|_2 \le(2\pi)^k\|\langle\xi\rangle^k h\|_2,\qquad h\in L^2 .$$
3. The three norm expressions are **not** identical in general: the
   bracket-weighted norm differs from both the weak-derivative norm and the
   Laplacian-weighted norm, as the Gaussian computation in the proof shows.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ be the Sobolev space of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]] with the weak gradient $\nabla u$ of
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]], write
$r(x):=|x|$, and write $\|u\|_2^2=\int_{\mathbb R^3}|u(x)|^2\,dx$ for the
$L^2$ norm of [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Then:

(a) for every $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\};\mathbb C)$,

$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{|u(x)|^2}{|x|^2}\,dx\le 4\int_{\mathbb R^3}|\nabla u(x)|^2\,dx;$$

(b) the same inequality holds for every $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$;

(c) for every $u\in W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ the a.e.-defined function $x\mapsto u(x)/|x|$ lies in $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ and satisfies $\|u/|\cdot|\|_2\le 2\|\nabla u\|_2$.

No constant smaller than $4$ is claimed, and no statement is made about
$\|u/|\cdot|\|_2$ for $u$ outside $W^{1,2}$.

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

Assume Countable Choice and let $n\ge1$. For every $u\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ and every multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$,
$$\mathcal F(D^\alpha u)=(2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\mathcal Fu\qquad\text{in }\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n),$$
where $D^\alpha$ is the distributional derivative of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]] and $\mathcal F$ is
the negative-sign $2\pi$-normalized transform. Moreover, if $u=u_f$ and
$D^\alpha u=u_g$ for $L^2$ classes $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb R^n)$ and their regular
distributions, then the unitary Plancherel transforms satisfy
$$\mathcal F_2g(\xi)=(2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\mathcal F_2f(\xi)\qquad\text{for almost every }\xi\in\mathbb R^n.$$
The second assertion compares the Plancherel classes only; it neither asserts
pointwise values of arbitrary representatives nor presupposes any Sobolev-space
notation.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Work on a complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in the first variable. Let $A$ be self-adjoint and let $B$ be symmetric with $D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ and
$A$-bound less than one ([[def-relative-boundedness-with-respect-to-an-operator]]).
Then $A+B$ with domain $D(A)$ is self-adjoint. If $A$ is merely essentially
self-adjoint and $B$ is symmetric with $D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ and $A$-bound less
than one, then $A+B$ on $D(A)$ is essentially self-adjoint and its closure is
the self-adjoint operator obtained by applying the first part to $\overline A$
and the graph-norm extension of $B|_{D(A)}$ to $D(\overline A)$. If $A\ge\gamma$ and
$(a,b)$ is an admissible pair for $B$ with $a<1$, then
$A+B\ge\gamma-\max\{a|\gamma|+b,\ b/(1-a)\}$.

Let $A$ be a linear operator on $H$ with domain $D(A)$. An operator $B$ is
**$A$-bounded**, or **relatively bounded with respect to $A$**, when
$D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ and there are finite constants $a,b\ge0$ with
$$\|Bx\|\le a\|Ax\|+b\|x\|\qquad\text{for all }x\in D(A).$$
The infimum of the admissible constants $a$ is the **$A$-bound** of $B$, and
one says the $A$-bound is *below one* when some $a<1$ is admissible.

**Equivalent form.** $B$ is $A$-bounded exactly when $B$ is bounded on $D(A)$
for the graph norm $\|x\|_A=(\|x\|^2+\|Ax\|^2)^{1/2}$ of

$\|Bx\|\le a\|Ax\|+b\|x\|$ gives
$\|Bx\|\le\max(a,b)\sqrt2\,\|x\|_A$, and conversely a graph-norm bound
$\|Bx\|\le C\|x\|_A$ gives the estimate with $a=b=C$. The constant $b$ is not

bounded for some, equivalently every, $z\in\rho(A)$

(a) For a real measurable finite-valued function $a:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ define $M_af:=af$ on $D(M_a):=\{f\in H: af\in H\}$. $$H_0:=\mathcal F_2^*\,M_{c|\xi|^2+b}\,\mathcal F_2,\qquad D(H_0):=\{f\in H:|\xi|^2\mathcal F_2f\in H\}.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $T$ be a
densely defined linear operator on $H$, with domain $D(T)$ dense in $H$
([[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]], [[def-dense-top]]).
Since $D(T)$ is dense, and since $H$ is complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]), every
bounded linear functional on the normed space $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]) extends uniquely to a bounded linear
functional $\widetilde\varphi$ on $H$ of the same norm, by setting
$\widetilde\varphi(z)=\lim_n\varphi(z_n)$ for any sequence $z_n\in D(T)$ with
$z_n\to z$ in $H$; the limit exists because $\varphi$ is bounded on a dense
subspace and $H$ is complete, and it does not depend on the sequence because a
bounded functional is uniformly continuous.

A vector $y\in H$ belongs to the **adjoint domain** $D(T^*)$ when the linear
functional $\varphi_y:D(T)\to\mathbb C$, $\varphi_y(x)=\langle Tx,y\rangle$, is
bounded on $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$. In that case Hilbert space Riesz representation
([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) applied to the extension
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$ produces a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with
$$T^*y\text{ is the unique }w\in H\text{ such that }\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,w\rangle\quad\text{for all }x\in D(T),$$
equivalently $\widetilde{\varphi_y}(z)=\langle z,T^*y\rangle$ for all $z\in H$.
The map $T^*:D(T^*)\to H$, $y\mapsto T^*y$, is the **adjoint** of $T$.

**Well-definedness.** The functional $\varphi_y$ is linear in $x$ for each
$y$, so its domain of boundedness $D(T^*)$ is a linear subspace: if
$\varphi_y,\varphi_{y'}$ are bounded so is $\varphi_{ay+by'}$ for scalars
$a,b$, because the first-variable-linear convention gives
$\varphi_{ay+by'}=\overline a\,\varphi_y+\overline b\,\varphi_{y'}$. On
$D(T^*)$ the map $T^*$ is linear: if $y,y'$ are represented by $w,w'$, then
$ay+by'$ is represented by $aw+bw'$, since
$\langle x,aw+bw'\rangle=\overline a\langle x,w\rangle+
\overline b\langle x,w'\rangle$; the representing vector is unique. By Riesz representation for the Hilbert space
$H$ a vector $w\in H$ is determined by the values $\langle z,w\rangle$ with
$z$ ranging over $H$, and those values are determined by the functional
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$. Equivalently, if $w,w'$ both represent $\varphi_y$,
then $\langle x,w-w'\rangle=0$ for every $x\in D(T)$; density of $D(T)$ and
continuity of the inner product extend this equality to every $x\in H$, and
taking $x=w-w'$ gives $w=w'$. Finally only
ambient-norm boundedness of $\varphi_y$ on $D(T)$ is required: no extension,
no closure and no closedness of $T$ is presupposed.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T$ be a densely defined linear operator on $H$.

- $T$ is **symmetric** when $T\subseteq T^*$, that is, $D(T)\subseteq D(T^*)$ and
  $Tx=T^*x$ for all $x\in D(T)$; equivalently
  $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,Ty\rangle$ for all $x,y\in D(T)$.
- $T$ is **self-adjoint** when $T=T^*$, that is, the domains and the values
  agree.
- $T$ is **essentially self-adjoint** when its closure $\overline T$ is
  self-adjoint; by [[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]] this presupposes
  that $T$ is closable.

**Consequences, with proofs.** These are part of the content of the definition.

1. *A symmetric $T$ is closable.* $T\subseteq T^*$ and $T^*$ is closed
   ([[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]]), so $T^*$ is a closed
   extension of $T$. In particular the closure $\overline T$ exists and
   $\overline T\subseteq T^*$.
2. *The closure of a symmetric operator is symmetric.* If $T\subseteq T^*$,
   the inclusion reversal of
   [[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]] applied to
   $T\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq T^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$. Applying it once more to the inclusion
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq(T^{**})^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^{***}$. Since $\overline T=T^{**}$ and
   $(\overline T)^*=T^{***}$
   ([[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]]), this reads
   $\overline T\subseteq(\overline T)^*$: the closure is symmetric. (Each
   application is legitimate because the adjoint is defined once its operator
   is densely defined, and $D(T^{**})$ is dense because
   $T\subseteq T^{**}=\overline T$, so that $D(T^{**})$ contains the dense
   domain $D(T)$.)
3. *A self-adjoint operator has no proper symmetric extension.* If $T=T^*$ and
   $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*$, then $S^*\subseteq T^*$ by inclusion reversal,
   so $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*\subseteq T^*=T$ and all inclusions are
   equalities.
4. *A self-adjoint operator is closed*, being equal to the adjoint $T^*$ of the
   densely defined $T$, and *an essentially self-adjoint operator has exactly
   one self-adjoint extension*, namely $\overline T$: a self-adjoint extension
   $S$ of $T$ is closed, hence contains the least closed extension
   $\overline T$, and then $S\subseteq S^*\subseteq(\overline T)^*=\overline T$
   by item 2 and symmetry, so $S=\overline T$.

derivations.claim: [Kinetic inequality] Let $u\in W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ and put $g:=\mathcal F_2u$. By [F3], $\|\nabla u\|_2^2=\int4\pi^2|\xi|^2|g(\xi)|^2\,d\xi$ and $\|\Delta u\|_2^2=\int(4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^2|g(\xi)|^2\,d\xi$, while $\|u\|_2^2=\int|g|^2$. Writing $4\pi^2|\xi|^2|g|^2=(|g|)(4\pi^2|\xi|^2|g|)$ and applying [F4] to the two factors gives $\|\nabla u\|_2^2\le\|u\|_2\|\Delta u\|_2$.

[Infinitesimal Coulomb bound] Combining step 1.1 with [F2] yields $\|u/|\cdot|\|_2\le2\|\nabla u\|_2\le2\sqrt{\|u\|_2\|\Delta u\|_2}$. For $\eta>0$ the arithmetic-geometric mean inequality $2\sqrt{ab}\le\eta a+\eta^{-1}b$ applied to $a=\|\Delta u\|_2$, $b=\|u\|_2$ gives $2\sqrt{\|u\|_2\|\Delta u\|_2}\le\eta\|\Delta u\|_2+\eta^{-1}\|u\|_2$. This proves (a).

[Relative bound of the multiplier] By [F6] applied to $a(x)=1/|x|$ (finite-valued on $\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ and arbitrary, say $0$, at the origin, a null set) the operator $M$ is self-adjoint on $D(M)=\{f:f/|\cdot|\in H\}$, and $M$ is symmetric on $D(M)$. Step 2.1 shows $D(H_0)=W^{2,2}\subseteq D(M)$ and $\|M u\|_2=\|u/|\cdot|\|_2\le\eta\|\Delta u\|_2+\eta^{-1}\|u\|_2=\eta\|H_0u\|_2+\eta^{-1}\|u\|_2$ for every $u\in D(H_0)$, since $\Delta u=-H_0u$ on $D(H_0)$ by [F1] and [F3]. Hence $(\eta,\eta^{-1})$ is an admissible pair for $M$ relative to $H_0$, and the $H_0$-bound of $M$ is zero; this is (b).

[Self-adjointness of the Coulomb operator] Fix $\gamma>0$ and let $\eta\in(0,1/\gamma)$. Then $B:=-\gamma M$ is symmetric with $D(H_0)\subseteq D(B)$ and admissible pair $(a,b)=(\gamma\eta,\gamma\eta^{-1})$ with $a<1$; indeed $\|Bu\|_2=\gamma\|Mu\|_2\le\gamma\eta\|H_0u\|_2+\gamma\eta^{-1}\|u\|_2$ by step 3.1. By [F5] with $A=H_0\ge0$ (so $\gamma_0=0$) the operator $C=H_0+B$ on $D(H_0)$ is self-adjoint with $C\ge-\max\{0,\ b/(1-a)\}=-\gamma\eta^{-1}/(1-\gamma\eta)$. Moreover $Cu=H_0u-\gamma u/|\cdot|=-\Delta u-\gamma u/|\cdot|$ for $u\in D(H_0)$, by [F1] and [F3]; this is (c).

boundaries.reason: The statement has no empty family, sum or limit index set; it quantifies over single vectors u and over eta > 0.

boundaries.evidence: u=0 satisfies both displayed inequalities with equality 0=0, and step 1.1 evaluates the Fourier integrals at g=0; the statement also fixes gamma > 0, excluding the trivial free case gamma=0 from the claim.
The admissible pair (eta, eta^{-1}) is symmetric and step 2.1 applies the arithmetic-geometric mean for every eta > 0, eta=1 included (pair (1,1)).

boundaries.reason: No degeneracy or multiplicity notion occurs. The threshold eta < 1/gamma in (c) is an open condition: the statement makes no claim at eta = 1/gamma, so no degenerate endpoint is asserted.

boundaries.evidence: The only endpoint is the singularity of 1/|x| at the origin, assigned the value 0 as stated; step 2.1 and the multiplier result used in step 3.1 integrate against it, and the origin is a Lebesgue-null set.
Countable Choice and Choice are assumed; the Fourier representation of H_0 and the multiplication form of step 1.1 use them as declared in the statement.

boundaries.reason: The result is an estimate plus an operator construction, not a biconditional; (b) and (c) are separate claims, not converses.
No converse is asserted; the statement explicitly makes no sharpness or optimality claim for the lower bound of C.

$H=L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ ([[def-hilbert-space]],
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), and let
$H_0:=-\Delta$ be the free operator of
[[thm-nrqm-composites-real-multipliers-and-free-bounded-potential-operators]]
with domain $D(H_0)=W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$
([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]): $H_0=\mathcal F_2^*M_{4\pi^2|\xi|^2}\mathcal F_2$
and $H_0u=-\Delta u$ for $u\in D(H_0)$, where $\Delta u$ is the distributional

$$M u:=\frac{u}{|\cdot|},\qquad D(M):=\Bigl\{u\in H:\frac{u}{|\cdot|}\in H\Bigr\},$$
and write $\|u\|_2=\|u\|_H$. Then:

(a) for every $u\in D(H_0)=W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ one has $u/|\cdot|\in L^2$ and

$$\Bigl\|\frac{u}{|\cdot|}\Bigr\|_2\le 2\sqrt{\|u\|_2\,\|\Delta u\|_2}\,,\qquad \Bigl\|\frac{u}{|\cdot|}\Bigr\|_2\le \eta\|\Delta u\|_2+\frac1\eta\|u\|_2\quad(\eta>0);$$

$$C:=H_0-\gamma M,\qquad D(C):=D(H_0)=W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C),$$

$C$, $H_0$, $\gamma$ or $\Delta$ is asserted.

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

Let $n\ge1$ and $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, with the componentwise integral and quotient conventions of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]. Define
$$\widehat f(\xi)=\mathcal Ff(\xi):=\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(x)\exp(-2\pi i x\cdot\xi)\,dx,\qquad \xi\in\mathbb R^n.$$
Here $x\cdot\xi=\sum_{j=1}^n x_j\xi_j$, Lebesgue measure is used, and the exponential is [[def-complex-exponential]]. Its unit modulus follows from [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]. The integral is evaluated using any measurable representative. Absolute convergence and representative independence are the obligations discharged by [[lem-l-one-fourier-transform-is-well-defined]]. The output is a function defined at every frequency, not merely an almost-everywhere class. At frequency zero the formula reads $\widehat f(0)=\int f$. No choice selection of representatives for a family of classes is part of this definition.

Assume countable choice. If $f,g\in\mathcal S$, their pointwise product and their everywhere-defined convolution are Schwartz functions, and
$$\mathcal F(f*g)=\widehat f\widehat g,\qquad\mathcal F(fg)=\widehat f*\widehat g.$$

Fix an integer $n\ge1$. With the complex smooth-function convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]] and multi-indices of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], define
$$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|,\qquad \mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)=\{f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C):p_{\alpha\beta}(f)<\infty\text{ for all }\alpha,\beta\}.$$
The zero multi-index gives $x^0=1$ and $\partial^0f=f$. These are actual smooth functions, not equivalence classes. The notation $C_c^\infty$ uses the support convention in [[def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn]].

Pointwise differentiation is linear; thus $p_{\alpha\beta}(f+g)\le p_{\alpha\beta}(f)+p_{\alpha\beta}(g)$ and $p_{\alpha\beta}(cf)=|c|p_{\alpha\beta}(f)$. In particular this set is a complex vector space and each $p_{\alpha\beta}$ is a seminorm. The zero function belongs to it. Since $p_{00}(f)=0$ forces $f(x)=0$ for every $x$, the family separates functions. No choice principle is needed.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Write
$L^2=L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ for the complex Hilbert space of Lebesgue
(equivalence classes of) square-integrable functions with inner product
$\langle f,g\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R^3}f\overline g$ linear in the first
argument ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]],
[[def-hilbert-space]]), and write $L^2(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$
for the same construction over the product with Lebesgue measure; identify
Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^6$ with the completion of the product of
Lebesgue measures on the two $\mathbb R^3$ factors.

**Kernel data and sections.** Let $k\in L^2(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$, an almost-everywhere equivalence class, and choose a finite-valued Lebesgue-measurable representative $k_0:\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb C$. When $f\in L^2$ is used, choose likewise a finite-valued Lebesgue-measurable representative $f_0:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb C$. For almost every $x\in\mathbb R^3$, the section $k_x(y):=k_0(x,y)$ is measurable, by applying the completed-product Fubini theorem to the positive and negative parts of the real and imaginary components of $k_0$ ([[thm-tonelli-and-fubini-for-completed-product-measures]]).

**Domain and action.** For $f\in L^2$ say that the integral defining $T_kf$
*exists at* $x\in\mathbb R^3$ if the section product
$y\mapsto k_0(x,y)f_0(y)$ is measurable and lies in $L^1(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$, and at such points put
$$(T_kf)(x):=\int_{\mathbb R^3}k_0(x,y)f_0(y)\,dy .$$
Define
$$D(T_k):=\Bigl\{f\in L^2:\ x\mapsto(T_kf)(x)\ \text{exists for almost every }x\text{ and agrees a.e. with a class in }L^2\Bigr\},$$
and for $f\in D(T_k)$ let $T_kf$ denote that class. The assignment
$f\mapsto T_kf$ is called the *$L^2$-kernel operator with kernel $k$*.

This definition is independent of both representative choices. If $k_1$ is
another representative of $k$, its disagreement set with $k_0$ is null for the
completed product Lebesgue measure. Fubini applied to the indicator of that
set gives $k_0(x,\cdot)=k_1(x,\cdot)$ almost everywhere for almost every
$x$. For each such $x$ and any representative of $f$, the two section products
therefore have the same $L^1$ status and, when integrable, the same integral.
Replacing $f_0$ by another representative changes the section product only on
a null set of $y$, so it too preserves integrability and the integral.
Consequently the almost-everywhere sections, the subset $D(T_k)\subseteq L^2$,
and the resulting output class are unchanged by either representative choice.

**Hilbert-Schmidt operators.** A linear operator $T$ on $L^2$ is called a
*Hilbert-Schmidt operator* if there is
$k\in L^2(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ with $D(T)=D(T_k)$ and
$T=T_k$; such a $k$ is called an *$L^2$ kernel* of $T$.

This definition asserts nothing about whether $D(T_k)$ is all of $L^2$,
whether $T_k$ is bounded, or whether $T_k$ is compact; those properties are
proved in [[lem-nrqm-coulomb-ltwo-kernel-operators-bounded-and-compact]]. A
finite product kernel $\sum_{i=1}^nf_i(x)\overline{g_i(y)}$ with
$f_i,g_i\in L^2$ is also a class in $L^2(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$,
as the same lemma records, so $T_k$ is defined for it whenever that membership
is used.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$L^2=L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ and let
$k\in L^2(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$, with $T_k$ the
$L^2$-kernel operator of [[def-nrqm-coulomb-ltwo-kernel-operators]]. Then:

(a) $D(T_k)=L^2$; $T_k$ is linear and bounded with
$\|T_kf\|_2\le\|k\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3)}\|f\|_2$ for every
$f\in L^2$, so $\|T_k\|\le\|k\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3)}$;

(b) if $n\ge1$, $f_1,\dots,f_n,g_1,\dots,g_n\in L^2$ and
$k(x,y)=\sum_{i=1}^nf_i(x)\overline{g_i(y)}$ a.e., then $k$ is a class in
$L^2(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$, the range of $T_k$ is contained
in $\operatorname{span}\{f_1,\dots,f_n\}$, and $T_k$ is compact;

(c) $T_k$ is compact; and

(d) for every sequence $(k_m)$ in
$L^2(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ with
$\|k_m-k\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3)}\to0$ one has
$T_{k_m}-T_k=T_{k_m-k}$ and
$\|T_{k_m}-T_k\|\le\|k_m-k\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3)}\to0$; in
particular $T_k$ is the operator-norm limit of finite-rank kernel operators.

No statement is made about the spectrum of $T_k$, about its singular values,
or about $L^2$ kernels of a given compact operator.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $W$, $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field. If
$T:X\to Y$ is compact ([[def-compact-linear-operator]]) and $A:W\to X$ and
$B:Y\to Z$ are bounded linear operators ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]), then
the composites $TA:W\to Y$ and $BT:X\to Z$ are compact.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[rem-real-and-complex-normed-space-convention]]. A linear map $T:X\to Y$
([[def-linear-map]]) is a **compact operator** when the image of every bounded
subset of $X$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has compact closure in $Y$
([[def-metric-compactness]]); explicitly, for every bounded $A\subseteq X$ the
closure $\overline{T(A)}$ in $Y$ is a compact subset of $Y$. The set of compact
operators $X\to Y$ is written $\mathcal K(X,Y)$.

**The closed unit ball suffices.** Put
$\overline B_X:=\{x\in X:\|x\|\le 1\}$
([[def-metric-ball]]). Then $T$ is compact if and only if
$\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a compact subset of $Y$.

Indeed, if $T$ is compact then $\overline B_X$ is bounded, because
$\overline B_X\subseteq B(0,2)$ while $B(0,2)$ is bounded and a subset of a
bounded set is bounded, so $T(\overline B_X)$ has compact closure. Conversely
assume $\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ compact and let $A\subseteq X$ be bounded.
If $A=\varnothing$ then $T(A)=\varnothing$, whose closure is empty and hence
compact. Otherwise $A\subseteq B(x_0,r)$ for some $x_0\in X$ and real $r>0$, so
every $x\in A$ satisfies $\|x\|\le\|x_0\|+r=:R$; if $R>0$ then
$A\subseteq R\,\overline B_X$ and if $R=0$ then $A\subseteq\{0\}$, so in either
case $T(A)\subseteq R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$. Scalar multiplication by
$R$ is continuous ([[lem-vector-operations-are-continuous-in-a-normed-space]]),
so $R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a compact subset of $Y$
([[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]), hence closed
([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]); therefore
$\overline{T(A)}\subseteq R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a closed subset of a
compact set, hence compact, and $T$ is compact.

**A compact operator is bounded.** If $T$ is compact then the compact set
$\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is bounded
([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]), so there is a real $C\ge0$ with
$\|Tx\|\le C$ for every $x\in\overline B_X$ and hence $\|Tx\|\le C\|x\|$ for
every $x\in X$; thus $T$ is a bounded linear operator
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). This is a consequence of compactness, not a
hypothesis of the definition.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $X$ be a
normed space, let $Y$ be a Banach space ([[def-banach-space]]), and let
$T_n:X\to Y$, $n\in\mathbb N$, be compact operators
([[def-compact-linear-operator]]) with $\|T_n-T\|\to0$ for a bounded linear
operator $T:X\to Y$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]],
[[def-operator-norm]], [[def-metric-convergence]]). Then $T$ is compact.
Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Every Schwartz function belongs to complex $L^2(\mathbb R^n)$, and the classes represented by $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ are dense there.

derivations.claim: [The resolvent as a Fourier multiplier] Fix $z\notin\mathbb R$ and define $m_z(\xi):=(4\pi^2|\xi|^2-z)^{-1}$. Since $|4\pi^2|\xi|^2-z|\ge|\operatorname{Im}z|$ one has $|m_z(\xi)|\le|\operatorname{Im}z|^{-1}$ everywhere; and whenever $4\pi^2|\xi|^2\ge2|\operatorname{Re}z|$ one has $|4\pi^2|\xi|^2-z|\ge4\pi^2|\xi|^2-|\operatorname{Re}z|\ge\tfrac12\,4\pi^2|\xi|^2$, so that $|m_z(\xi)|\le\frac1{2\pi^2|\xi|^2}$. With $\rho:=\max\{1,\sqrt{2|\operatorname{Re}z|}/(2\pi)\}>0$, so that $4\pi^2\rho^2\ge2|\operatorname{Re}z|$ this yields $\int_{\mathbb R^3}|m_z|^2\le|\operatorname{Im}z|^{-2}\,|B(0,\rho)|+\frac1{4\pi^4}\int_{|\xi|>\rho}|\xi|^{-4}d\xi<\infty$, because $\int_{|\xi|>\rho}|\xi|^{-4}d\xi=4\pi\int_\rho^\infty r^{-2}dr$; so $m_z\in L^2(\mathbb R^3)$; moreover $m_z(\xi)(4\pi^2|\xi|^2-z)=1$ for a.e. $\xi$. Define $R_0(z):=\mathcal F_2^*M_{m_z}\mathcal F_2$; then for $f\in L^2$ the vector $R_0(z)f$ lies in $D(H_0)$, because $|\xi|^2m_z(\xi)\mathcal F_2f(\xi)=(\mathcal F_2f(\xi)+zm_z(\xi)\mathcal F_2f(\xi))/(4\pi^2)$ is a sum of two $L^2$ functions, and $(H_0-z)R_0(z)f=f$ since $\mathcal F_2((H_0-z)R_0(z)f)=(4\pi^2|\xi|^2-z)m_z(\xi)\mathcal F_2f=\mathcal F_2f$; conversely for $g\in D(H_0)$ the function $(4\pi^2|\xi|^2-z)\mathcal F_2g$ is in $L^2$, so $R_0(z)(H_0-z)g$ is defined and its transform is $m_z(\xi)(4\pi^2|\xi|^2-z)\mathcal F_2g=\mathcal F_2g$. Hence $R_0(z)=(H_0-z)^{-1}$ and $\|R_0(z)\|\le|\operatorname{Im}z|^{-1}$.

[$L^\infty$ bound of the free resolvent] For Schwartz $f$ the function $m_z\mathcal F_2f$ lies in $L^1\cap L^2$, so $R_0(z)f$ has the everywhere-defined representative $x\mapsto\int m_z(\xi)\mathcal F_2f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}d\xi$, whose modulus is at most $\|m_z\|_2\|\mathcal F_2f\|_2=\|m_z\|_2\|f\|_2$ by [F7]. For general $f\in L^2$ choose Schwartz $f_n\to f$ in $L^2$; then $R_0(z)f_n\to R_0(z)f$ in $L^2$ and $\|R_0(z)f_n-R_0(z)f_m\|_\infty\le\|m_z\|_2\|f_n-f_m\|_2$, so the representatives converge uniformly to a bounded function $h$ with $\|h\|_\infty\le\|m_z\|_2\|f\|_2$; uniform convergence gives $L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$ convergence and hence $h=R_0(z)f$ a.e., so $\|R_0(z)f\|_\infty\le\|m_z\|_2\|f\|_2$.

[Convolution kernel] Put $g_z:=\mathcal F_2^*m_z\in L^2$ by [F3]. We first prove $R_0(z)f=g_z*f$ for Schwartz $f$. Choose Schwartz functions $\varphi_n$ with $\varphi_n\to g_z$ in $L^2$ ([F10]). For every $n$ both $\varphi_n$ and $f$ are Schwartz, so [F4] gives $\mathcal F_2(\varphi_n*f)=\widehat{\varphi_n}\widehat f$; here $\widehat{\varphi_n}\to\mathcal F_2g_z=m_z$ in $L^2$ by the isometry [F3], while $|\widehat f(\xi)|\le\|f\|_1<\infty$ for every $\xi$ by the defining integral of the $L^1$ transform [F3] and the integrability of the Schwartz function $f$; hence $\mathcal F_2(\varphi_n*f)=\widehat{\varphi_n}\widehat f\to m_z\widehat f=\mathcal F_2(R_0(z)f)$ in $L^2$. Since $\mathcal F_2$ is an isometry, $\varphi_n*f\to R_0(z)f$ in $L^2$. On the other hand $\varphi_n*f\to g_z*f$ in $L^2$: for $h:=\varphi_n-g_z$ and a.e. $x$, $\int|h(x-y)||f(y)|dy=\int|h(x-y)|\sqrt{|f(y)|}\sqrt{|f(y)|}dy\le\bigl(\int|h(x-y)|^2|f(y)|dy\bigr)^{1/2}\|f\|_1^{1/2}$ by [F7], so Tonelli [F6] gives $\|h*f\|_2^2\le\|f\|_1\iint|h(x-y)|^2|f(y)|dydx=\|f\|_1^2\|h\|_2^2\to0$. Therefore $R_0(z)f=g_z*f$ for Schwartz $f$. This identity also gives $\|g_z*f\|_2=\|R_0(z)f\|_2=\|m_z\mathcal F_2f\|_2\le\|m_z\|_\infty\|f\|_2$ for Schwartz $f$, so $f\mapsto g_z*f$ is bounded on the dense subspace of Schwartz classes and extends uniquely to a bounded operator on $L^2$ by [F10], and this extension agrees with the bounded operator $R_0(z)$ on the dense subspace; hence the extension equals $R_0(z)$ on every $f\in L^2$. It also equals the ordinary convolution representative: for fixed $x$, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\int|g_z(x-y)f(y)|dy\le\|g_z\|_2\|f\|_2$, and for Schwartz $f_n\to f$ it gives $\sup_x|g_z*(f_n-f)(x)|\le\|g_z\|_2\|f_n-f\|_2\to0$. This is uniform convergence, while $R_0(z)f_n\to R_0(z)f$ in $L^2$. On every bounded set both limits agree by $L^2$ convergence and uniform convergence, proving $R_0(z)f=g_z*f$ almost everywhere for the ordinary convolution as well.

[Localized resolvent is Hilbert–Schmidt] Let $\chi$ be bounded with compact support. By step 2.2, $M_\chi R_0(z)f=\chi\cdot(g_z*f)$, so the operator $M_\chi R_0(z)$ has the kernel $k(x,y):=\chi(x)g_z(x-y)$. The function $k$ is product-measurable and $\int\int|k(x,y)|^2dx\,dy=\int|\chi(x)|^2\Bigl(\int|g_z(x-y)|^2dy\Bigr)dx=\|\chi\|_2^2\|g_z\|_2^2<\infty$ by [F6]; hence $M_\chi R_0(z)=T_k$ is Hilbert–Schmidt in the sense of [[def-nrqm-coulomb-ltwo-kernel-operators]] and compact by [F5].

[Short-range and tail estimates] For $\varepsilon>0$ let $B_\varepsilon:=\{x:|x|<\varepsilon\}$. By step 2.1, $\|M_{\gamma|\cdot|^{-1}\mathbf 1_{B_\varepsilon}}R_0(z)f\|_2\le\gamma\Bigl(\int_{B_\varepsilon}|x|^{-2}dx\Bigr)^{1/2}\|R_0(z)f\|_\infty\le\gamma\sqrt{4\pi\varepsilon}\,\|m_z\|_2\|f\|_2$, so the operator norm is at most $\gamma\sqrt{4\pi\varepsilon}\|m_z\|_2$. For $R>0$, $\|M_{\gamma|\cdot|^{-1}\mathbf 1_{\{|x|>R\}}}R_0(z)\|\le\gamma R^{-1}\|R_0(z)\|\le\gamma R^{-1}|\operatorname{Im}z|^{-1}$.

[Compactness of $MR_0(z)$] Fix $R>\varepsilon>0$ and choose a bounded measurable $\chi$ with $0\le\chi\le1$, $\chi=1$ on $\{\varepsilon\le|x|\le R\}$ and $\chi=0$ off $\{\varepsilon/2\le|x|\le2R\}$; this is possible with compact support. Since $\chi=1$ on the closed annulus $\{\varepsilon\le|x|\le R\}$, the function $1-\chi$ vanishes there and satisfies the pointwise domination $0\le\gamma\frac{1-\chi(x)}{|x|}\le\gamma\frac{\mathbf 1_{B_\varepsilon}(x)}{|x|}+\gamma\frac{\mathbf 1_{\{|x|>R\}}(x)}{|x|}$. Hence $\gamma MR_0(z)=M_{\gamma|\cdot|^{-1}\chi}R_0(z)+M_{\gamma|\cdot|^{-1}(1-\chi)}R_0(z)$, where the first summand is compact by step 3.1 and the second has operator norm at most $\gamma\sqrt{4\pi\varepsilon}\|m_z\|_2+\gamma R^{-1}|\operatorname{Im}z|^{-1}$ by step 3.2, because its multiplier is pointwise dominated by the sum of the two multipliers of step 3.2. Given $\delta>0$ choose $\varepsilon$ and $R$ making this bound smaller than $\delta$. Thus $\gamma MR_0(z)$ lies within $\delta$ of a compact operator for every $\delta>0$, hence is compact by [F9].

[Conclusion] By step 4.1 and [F8], $VR_0(z)=-\gamma MR_0(z)$ is compact; the graph-norm boundedness of $V$ with respect to $H_0$ is [F2]. Hence $V$ is $H_0$-compact in the sense of [[def-relative-compactness-with-respect-to-an-operator]], and the equivalent formulations in (a)–(c) are steps 1.1, 2.1, 2.2 and 3.1.

boundaries.reason: No empty family occurs; chi ranges over bounded compactly supported measurable functions, a nonempty class containing 0.

boundaries.evidence: The statement assumes gamma > 0, so the perturbation V = -gamma M is not the zero operator; step 4.1 factors gamma explicitly and no claim is made for gamma = 0. The zero chi is allowed in step 3.1 but is not used for the compactness conclusion.
chi = 1 on the annulus is the indicator case used in step 4.1; the Hilbert-Schmidt estimate of step 3.1 applies to every bounded compactly supported chi including indicators.

boundaries.reason: No degeneracy notion occurs; the resolvent parameter z is confined to the resolvent set C minus R, where no degeneracy of m_z = (4 pi^2 |xi|^2 - z)^{-1} can occur.

boundaries.evidence: The two spatial endpoints are the origin and infinity: step 3.2 bounds the short-range piece by int_{B_eps} |x|^{-2} dx and the tail piece by the L^infinity estimate of step 2.1, and step 4.1 combines them in the norm limit, so neither is neglected.
Countable Choice and Choice are assumed; step 3.2 chooses epsilon > 0 and step 4.1 chooses the annulus parameters R > epsilon, countably many explicit choices as declared.

boundaries.reason: The claim is not a biconditional; H_0-compactness is established in one direction only.
No converse is claimed: the statement explicitly makes no assertion about compactness of M itself.
