[[thm-the-l-p-distance-for-zero-less-p-less-one-is-a-complete-translation-invariant-metric]]
supplies the metric structure rather than a normed-space structure.

Assume countable choice. If $f,g\in\mathcal S$, their pointwise product and their everywhere-defined convolution are Schwartz functions, and
$$\mathcal F(f*g)=\widehat f\widehat g,\qquad\mathcal F(fg)=\widehat f*\widehat g.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $X$ be a normed space, let $D \subseteq X$ be a dense normed subspace, let
$Y$ be a Banach space, and let $T:D\to Y$ be a bounded linear operator. Then
there is a unique bounded linear operator $\widetilde T:X\to Y$ such that

$$\widetilde T|_D = T,$$

and $\|\widetilde T\| = \|T\|$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), let $d\ge1$ and work on $H=L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ ([[def-hilbert-space]]).

(a) For a real measurable finite-valued function $a:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ define $M_af:=af$ on $D(M_a):=\{f\in H: af\in H\}$. Then $M_a$ is a densely defined self-adjoint operator on $H$ ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]).

(b) Let $c>0$, $b\in\mathbb R$, and let $\mathcal F_2$ be the unitary Plancherel transform with the convention $\widehat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}dx$ on $L^1$ ([[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]], [[thm-plancherel]]). Define

$$H_0:=\mathcal F_2^*\,M_{c|\xi|^2+b}\,\mathcal F_2,\qquad D(H_0):=\{f\in H:|\xi|^2\mathcal F_2f\in H\}.$$

Then $H_0$ is self-adjoint, $D(H_0)$ coincides with the Sobolev space $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ as a set (with equivalent norms, [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[thm-fourier-characterisation-of-integer-order-hilbert-sobolev-spaces]]), $H_0\ge b$ in the quadratic-form sense, and for every Schwartz function $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, $H_0f=-(c/4\pi^2)\Delta f+bf$.

(c) If $V:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ is measurable with $\|V\|_\infty<\infty$ and $H:=H_0+M_V$ with domain $D(H_0)$, then $H$ is self-adjoint on $D(H_0)$, is bounded below, and the assignment $t\mapsto e^{itH}$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group whose generator is $iH$: the limit $\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t(e^{itH}\psi-\psi)$ exists exactly for $\psi\in D(H)$ and equals $iH\psi$ ([[lem-self-adjoint-operator-generates-a-strongly-continuous-unitary-group]]).

(d) *Scope*: the argument uses only boundedness and measurability of $V$; it proves nothing for $V\propto-1/|x|$, $V\propto|x|^2$ or the delta interaction, does not identify $H_0$ with any measured free-particle Hamiltonian, and asserts no physical interpretation.

Assume Countable Choice, let $n\ge1$ and $k\in\mathbb N_0$, and use complex
scalars. Write $W^{k,2}=W^{k,2}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ for the weak-derivative
Sobolev space of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], whose classes carry
the weak derivatives $D^\alpha f\in L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ for
$|\alpha|\le k$ and the norm
$$\|f\|_{W^{k,2}}=\Bigl(\sum_{|\alpha|\le k}\|D^\alpha f\|_2^2\Bigr)^{1/2},$$
and let $H^k=H^k(\mathbb R^n)$ be the real-order Bessel-potential completion
of [[def-real-order-bessel-potential-sobolev-space]] with its canonical
embedding $E_k:H^k\to\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$
([[thm-bessel-potential-completions-embed-in-tempered-distributions]]). Let
$u_f\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ denote the regular tempered distribution of
an $L^2$ class $f$. Then:

1. $E_k[H^k]=\{u_f:f\in W^{k,2}\}$, and
   $\Phi(f):=E_k^{-1}(u_f)$ is a bijection
   $\Phi:W^{k,2}\to H^k$. Thus, under the regular-distribution embedding,
   $W^{k,2}$ and $H^k$ are the same subspace of $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$.
2. There are constants $0<c_k\le C_k<\infty$, depending only on $n$ and $k$,
   with
$$c_k^{1/2}\,\|\langle\xi\rangle^k\mathcal F_2f\|_2\le\|f\|_{W^{k,2}} \le C_k^{1/2}\,\|\langle\xi\rangle^k\mathcal F_2f\|_2,$$
   and $\|\langle\xi\rangle^k\mathcal F_2f\|_2=\|\Phi(f)\|_{H^k}$. Hence the
   weak-derivative norm and the bracket-weighted $L^2$ norm are equivalent,
   and the latter is also equivalent to
   $\|(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{k/2}\mathcal F_2f\|_2$, by
$$\|\langle\xi\rangle^k h\|_2\le\|(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{k/2}h\|_2 \le(2\pi)^k\|\langle\xi\rangle^k h\|_2,\qquad h\in L^2 .$$
3. The three norm expressions are **not** identical in general: the
   bracket-weighted norm differs from both the weak-derivative norm and the
   Laplacian-weighted norm, as the Gaussian computation in the proof shows.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Work on a complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in the first variable. Let $A$ be self-adjoint and let $B$ be symmetric with $D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ and
$A$-bound less than one ([[def-relative-boundedness-with-respect-to-an-operator]]).
Then $A+B$ with domain $D(A)$ is self-adjoint. If $A$ is merely essentially
self-adjoint and $B$ is symmetric with $D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ and $A$-bound less
than one, then $A+B$ on $D(A)$ is essentially self-adjoint and its closure is
the self-adjoint operator obtained by applying the first part to $\overline A$
and the graph-norm extension of $B|_{D(A)}$ to $D(\overline A)$. If $A\ge\gamma$ and
$(a,b)$ is an admissible pair for $B$ with $a<1$, then
$A+B\ge\gamma-\max\{a|\gamma|+b,\ b/(1-a)\}$.

Let $A$ be a linear operator on $H$ with domain $D(A)$. An operator $B$ is
**$A$-bounded**, or **relatively bounded with respect to $A$**, when
$D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ and there are finite constants $a,b\ge0$ with
$$\|Bx\|\le a\|Ax\|+b\|x\|\qquad\text{for all }x\in D(A).$$
The infimum of the admissible constants $a$ is the **$A$-bound** of $B$, and
one says the $A$-bound is *below one* when some $a<1$ is admissible.

**Equivalent form.** $B$ is $A$-bounded exactly when $B$ is bounded on $D(A)$
for the graph norm $\|x\|_A=(\|x\|^2+\|Ax\|^2)^{1/2}$ of
[[def-unbounded-linear-operator-domain-and-graph]]: each estimate
$\|Bx\|\le a\|Ax\|+b\|x\|$ gives
$\|Bx\|\le\max(a,b)\sqrt2\,\|x\|_A$, and conversely a graph-norm bound
$\|Bx\|\le C\|x\|_A$ gives the estimate with $a=b=C$. The constant $b$ is not
intrinsic, and no closedness, density or resolvent hypothesis is needed for
the definition. If $A$ is closed with nonempty resolvent set, then $A$-bounded
operators are exactly those with $D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ for which $BR_A(z)$ is
bounded for some, equivalently every, $z\in\rho(A)$
([[def-resolvent-and-spectrum-of-a-closed-unbounded-operator]]). Indeed, an
$A$-bound makes $BR_A(z)$ bounded because
$AR_A(z)=zR_A(z)-I$; conversely, if $BR_A(z)$ is bounded, then
$Bx=BR_A(z)(z-A)x$ gives an $A$-bound. Thus boundedness for one resolvent
implies relative boundedness and hence boundedness for every resolvent. This
is used in the Kato-Rellich theorem below and recorded here as an interface.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\gamma>0$, let
$H=L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ ([[def-hilbert-space]],
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), and let
$H_0:=-\Delta$ be the free operator of
[[thm-nrqm-composites-real-multipliers-and-free-bounded-potential-operators]]
with domain $D(H_0)=W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$
([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]): $H_0=\mathcal F_2^*M_{4\pi^2|\xi|^2}\mathcal F_2$
and $H_0u=-\Delta u$ for $u\in D(H_0)$, where $\Delta u$ is the distributional
Laplacian. Write $M$ for the multiplication operator
$$M u:=\frac{u}{|\cdot|},\qquad D(M):=\Bigl\{u\in H:\frac{u}{|\cdot|}\in H\Bigr\},$$
and write $\|u\|_2=\|u\|_H$. Then:

(a) for every $u\in D(H_0)=W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ one has $u/|\cdot|\in L^2$ and

$$\Bigl\|\frac{u}{|\cdot|}\Bigr\|_2\le 2\sqrt{\|u\|_2\,\|\Delta u\|_2}\,,\qquad \Bigl\|\frac{u}{|\cdot|}\Bigr\|_2\le \eta\|\Delta u\|_2+\frac1\eta\|u\|_2\quad(\eta>0);$$

(b) $M$ is a self-adjoint operator on $H$ with $D(H_0)\subseteq D(M)$, symmetric on $D(H_0)$, with $H_0$-bound zero in the sense that for every $\eta>0$ the pair $(\eta,\eta^{-1})$ is admissible for $M$ relative to $H_0$;

(c) for every $\gamma>0$ the operator
$$C:=H_0-\gamma M,\qquad D(C):=D(H_0)=W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C),$$
is self-adjoint on $H$, bounded below, and acts by $Cu=-\Delta u-\gamma u/|\cdot|$ for every $u\in D(C)$; for every $\eta\in(0,1/\gamma)$ one has $C\ge-\gamma\eta^{-1}/(1-\gamma\eta)$ in the quadratic-form sense.

No sharp lower bound of $C$ is claimed here, and no physical interpretation of
$C$, $H_0$, $\gamma$ or $\Delta$ is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ be the Sobolev space of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]] with the weak gradient $\nabla u$ of
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]], write
$r(x):=|x|$, and write $\|u\|_2^2=\int_{\mathbb R^3}|u(x)|^2\,dx$ for the
$L^2$ norm of [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Then:

(a) for every $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\};\mathbb C)$,

$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{|u(x)|^2}{|x|^2}\,dx\le 4\int_{\mathbb R^3}|\nabla u(x)|^2\,dx;$$

(b) the same inequality holds for every $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$;

(c) for every $u\in W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ the a.e.-defined function $x\mapsto u(x)/|x|$ lies in $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ and satisfies $\|u/|\cdot|\|_2\le 2\|\nabla u\|_2$.

No constant smaller than $4$ is claimed, and no statement is made about
$\|u/|\cdot|\|_2$ for $u$ outside $W^{1,2}$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\gamma>0$, and for
every $l\ge0$ let $A_l$ be the radial operator of
[[thm-nrqm-coulomb-transported-radial-endpoint-realization]]; let
$C=-\Delta-\gamma/|\cdot|$ on $D(C)=H^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ be the
self-adjoint operator of [[thm-nrqm-coulomb-infinitesimal-kinetic-bound]] (c),
with essential spectrum $[0,\infty)$
([[thm-nrqm-coulomb-essential-spectrum]]), and let $U$ be the polar unitary of
[[thm-nrqm-coulomb-transported-radial-endpoint-realization]] (d). Then:

(a) if $k>0$ and $j:=\gamma/(2k)-l-1\notin\mathbb N_0$, then the regular solution $u_{\mathrm{reg}}$ of [[thm-nrqm-coulomb-kummer-recurrence-and-termination]] is not square-integrable on $(0,\infty)$, and $-k^2$ is not an eigenvalue of $A_l$;

(b) the negative eigenvalues of $A_l$ are exactly the numbers
$$-\frac{\gamma^2}{4n^2},\qquad n\ge l+1,$$
each with one-dimensional eigenspace spanned by the corresponding regular solution $u_{\mathrm{reg}}$; in particular every negative eigenvalue of $A_l$ is simple;

(c) the negative eigenvalues of $C$ are exactly the numbers $-\gamma^2/(4n^2)$ with $n\ge1$;

(d) every eigenfunction of $C$ with negative eigenvalue lies in the closed span of the transported regular solutions: if $C\psi=E\psi$ with $E<0$ and $U\psi=(u_{lm})$, then $E=-\gamma^2/(4n^2)$ for some $n\ge1$, and each nonzero $u_{lm}$ is a scalar multiple of the regular solution of $A_l$ at that energy.

This exhausts the negative spectrum of $A_l$ and of $C$ by the terminating
Laguerre solutions; no claim is made here about completeness of these
eigenfunctions in the negative spectral subspace, about the multiplicity of
the levels of $C$, or about any physical interpretation.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\gamma>0$ and let
$C=-\Delta-\gamma/|\cdot|$ on $D(C)=H^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ be the
self-adjoint operator of [[thm-nrqm-coulomb-infinitesimal-kinetic-bound]] with
essential spectrum $[0,\infty)$. For $n\ge1$, $0\le l\le n-1$ and
$-l\le m\le l$ let $u_{nl}$ be the regular solution of
[[thm-nrqm-coulomb-kummer-recurrence-and-termination]] at $k=\gamma/(2n)$
(the polynomial-exponential solution, unique up to a nonzero scalar), and put
$$\psi_{nlm}(x):=\frac{u_{nl}(r)}{r}Y_{lm}(\Omega)\qquad(x=r\Omega).$$
Then:

(a) each $\psi_{nlm}$ lies in $D(C)$ and $C\psi_{nlm}=-\frac{\gamma^2}{4n^2}\psi_{nlm}$; the vectors $\psi_{nlm}$ with distinct labels are pairwise orthogonal, and for fixed $n$ the eigenspace of $C$ at $-\gamma^2/(4n^2)$ is exactly their span; it has dimension $\sum_{l=0}^{n-1}(2l+1)=n^2$;

(b) after normalization, the family $(\psi_{nlm}/\|u_{nl}\|_2)_{n\ge1,0\le l\le n-1,-l\le m\le l}$ is a complete orthonormal family of the negative spectral subspace $E_C((-\infty,0))L^2(\mathbb R^3)$;

(c) the family is not complete in $L^2(\mathbb R^3)$: the nonnegative spectral subspace $E_C([0,\infty))L^2(\mathbb R^3)$ is nonzero (indeed infinite dimensional), so the bound states alone do not span $L^2$.

All claims concern the mathematical spectral decomposition of $C$; no physical
interpretation is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), let $a,b\ge1$ and identify $\mathbb R^{a+b}=\mathbb R^a\times\mathbb R^b$ with Lebesgue measure ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]); write $H_a=L^2(\mathbb R^a)$, $H_b=L^2(\mathbb R^b)$. Then there is a unique linear isometry

$$\Theta:H_a\widehat\otimes H_b\longrightarrow L^2(\mathbb R^{a+b})$$

with $\Theta(f\otimes g)(x,y)=f(x)g(y)$ for all $f\in H_a$, $g\in H_b$ and a.e. $(x,y)$, and $\Theta$ is onto: it is a surjective linear isometry, hence unitary. Vector-valued or spin factors follow by finite component sums. No identification of non-Euclidean product measures is asserted.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\gamma\ge0$, $l\ge0$,
let $A_l$ be the radial operator of
[[thm-nrqm-coulomb-transported-radial-endpoint-realization]] with spectral
measure $E_{A_l}$, and for $k>0$ let $\varphi_l(k,\cdot)$ and $f_l(k,\cdot)$
be the solutions of [[thm-nrqm-coulomb-jost-volterra-solution]], with
$W_l(k):=W(\varphi_l(k,\cdot),f_l(k,\cdot))\ne0$. Write
$$\rho_l(E):=\frac{\sqrt E}{\pi\,|W_l(\sqrt E)|^2}\qquad(E>0).$$

For $g\in L^2(0,\infty)$ write $\mu_g(B):=\langle E_{A_l}(B)g,g\rangle$
for its finite positive scalar spectral measure, where $B\subseteq\mathbb R$
is Borel ([[def-projection-valued-measure]],
[[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]). A finite
positive Borel measure $\mu$ is *absolutely continuous* with respect to
Lebesgue measure $dE$ if $\mu(N)=0$ for every Borel set $N$ of Lebesgue measure
zero; it is *singular continuous* if it is carried by a Borel Lebesgue-null
set and has no atoms, meaning $\mu(\{E\})=0$ for every $E\in\mathbb R$.
Define the absolutely continuous subspace
$$\mathcal H_{\mathrm{ac}}(A_l):=\{g\in L^2(0,\infty):\mu_g\text{ is absolutely continuous with respect to }dE\}.$$
It is a closed linear subspace because it equals
$\bigcap_{N:\,|N|=0}\ker E_{A_l}(N)$, where the intersection is over Borel
Lebesgue-null sets and $\mu_g(N)=\|E_{A_l}(N)g\|^2$.
For $I=(0,\infty)$, put
$$\mathcal H_{\mathrm{sc}}(A_l;I):=\{g\in E_{A_l}(I)L^2(0,\infty):\mu_g\text{ is singular continuous}\}.$$
The set $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{sc}}(A_l;I)$ is a closed linear subspace:
linear combinations of such vectors have scalar measures supported on the
union of their null carriers and have no atoms, and these two properties pass
to limits of vectors by continuity of the PVM projections. Here $E_{A_l}(I)L^2$ is
*purely absolutely continuous* when it is contained in $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{ac}}(A_l)$,
and “$A_l$ has no singular-continuous spectrum on $I$” means
$\mathcal H_{\mathrm{sc}}(A_l;I)=\{0\}$. Thus each operator spectral-type
phrase in (d) is a statement about the scalar PVM measures, not an additional
pointwise classification of energies.

Then:

(a) *resolvent kernel.* For $z=k^2$ with $\operatorname{Im}k>0$ and $k$ in the domain of the Jost construction, and for every $g\in L^2(0,\infty)$ with compact support, the resolvent is given by
$$((A_l-z)^{-1}g)(r)=\int_0^\infty G_l(r,s)g(s)\,ds,\qquad G_l(r,s):=-\frac{\varphi_l(k,\min(r,s))\,f_l(k,\max(r,s))}{W_l(k)},$$
and $G_l$ solves $(A_l-z)G_l=\delta$ in the sense that $-G''+(l(l+1)/r^2-\gamma/r)G-zG=0$ away from $r=s$ and the derivative of $G$ has the jump $-1$ at $r=s$; moreover $\|(A_l-z)^{-1}\|\le1/|\operatorname{Im}z|$;

(b) *boundary value.* For real $k>0$ one has $\varphi_l(k,\cdot)$ real and, for all $r,s>0$,
$$\operatorname{Im}G_l(k^2+i0;r,s)=\frac{k\,\varphi_l(k,r)\varphi_l(k,s)}{|W_l(k)|^2};$$

(c) *spectral density.* For every $g\in L^2(0,\infty)$ and every $0<a<b$,
$$\langle E_{A_l}((a,b))g,g\rangle=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\frac1\pi\int_a^b\operatorname{Im}\bigl\langle(A_l-E-i\varepsilon)^{-1}g,g\bigr\rangle dE,$$
and if $g$ has compact support then
$$\langle E_{A_l}((a,b))g,g\rangle=\int_a^b\rho_l(E)\Bigl|\int_0^\infty\varphi_l(\sqrt E,r)g(r)\,dr\Bigr|^2dE;$$
consequently for compactly supported $g$ the measure $E_{A_l,g}(B):=\langle E_{A_l}(B)g,g\rangle$ restricted to $(0,\infty)$ is absolutely continuous with density $\rho_l(E)|\int\varphi_l g|^2$;

(d) *absolutely continuous spectrum; no zero eigenvalue.* For every $g\in L^2(0,\infty)$ the measure $E_{A_l,g}$ has no atom in $(0,\infty)$; the positive spectral subspace $E_{A_l}((0,\infty))L^2(0,\infty)$ is purely absolutely continuous and is the closed span of the positive spectral projections of compactly supported functions; it equals the absolutely continuous subspace of $A_l$, and $A_l$ has no singular continuous spectrum on $(0,\infty)$; moreover $0$ is not an eigenvalue of $A_l$.

No scattering phase, normalization of the continuum functions as a unitary
transform, or physical cross-section is asserted; the transform itself is the
subject of the companion item [[thm-nrqm-coulomb-onto-radial-continuum-transform]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\gamma\ge0$, $l\ge0$,
and let $A_l$ be the radial operator of
[[thm-nrqm-coulomb-transported-radial-endpoint-realization]] with form domain
$V_l$. Fix $k_{\min}>0$ and let $K:=\{k\in\mathbb C:\operatorname{Re}k\ge k_{\min},\ \operatorname{Im}k\ge0\}$.
Then:

(a) *regular solution.* With $c_0:=1$, $c_{-1}:=0$ and
$$c_n:=-\frac{\gamma c_{n-1}+k^2c_{n-2}}{n(n+2l+1)}\qquad(n\ge1),$$
the series $\varphi_l(k,r):=r^{l+1}\sum_{n\ge0}c_nr^n$ converges for every $r>0$ and every $k\in\mathbb C$, the function $(k,r)\mapsto\varphi_l(k,r)$ is holomorphic in $k$ and $C^\infty$ in $r>0$, and $\varphi_l$ solves $-u''+\bigl(l(l+1)/r^2-\gamma/r\bigr)u=k^2u$ with $\varphi_l(k,r)/r^{l+1}\to1$ as $r\downarrow0$;

(b) *Jost-type solution.* Put $a:=\gamma/(2k)$, $\theta(r):=kr+a\log r$, $w(r):=e^{i\theta(r)}$, $b:=a^2+l(l+1)+ia$ and consider the integral equation
$$v(r)=1+\int_r^\infty\frac{b}{s^2}\,w(s)^2\Bigl(\int_r^sw(y)^{-2}dy\Bigr)v(s)\,ds .$$
For every $k\in K$ with $k\ne0$ the equation has exactly one bounded solution $v(\cdot;k)$ on $[r_0,\infty)$ for some $r_0>0$ depending on $k$, and $v(r)=1+O(1/r)$, $v'(r)=O(1/r)$; the functions $f_l(k,r):=w(r)v(r)$ and $v$ are continuous on $K$, holomorphic in $k$ for $\operatorname{Im}k>0$, satisfy the radial equation $-\partial_r^2f_l+\bigl(l(l+1)/r^2-\gamma/r\bigr)f_l=k^2f_l$ exactly, and obey the asymptotics
$$f_l=e^{i(kr+a\log r)}(1+O(1/r)),\qquad f_l'=e^{i(kr+a\log r)}[ik+O(1/r)]\qquad(r\to\infty);$$

(c) *Wronskians.* For real $k>0$ one has $W(\overline{f_l},f_l)=2ik$ and $W_l(k):=W(\varphi_l,f_l)\ne0$; consequently every solution of the radial equation on $(0,\infty)$ is $Af_l+B\overline{f_l}$ with $A,B\in\mathbb C$, and $\varphi_l$ is a nonzero complex multiple combination of $f_l,\overline{f_l}$;

(d) *no positive eigenvalue.* For real $k>0$ and $A,B\in\mathbb C$, if $g=Af_l+B\overline{f_l}$ then $\int_R^L|g(r)|^2dr=(|A|^2+|B|^2)[L-R-\gamma\log(L/R)/(2k^2)]+O(1)$ as $L\to\infty$ with $R>r_0$ fixed; hence $g\in L^2(r_0,\infty)$ if and only if $A=B=0$, and $k^2>0$ is not an eigenvalue of $A_l$.

All assertions concern the ordinary differential equation and the operator
$A_l$; no scattering amplitude, cross-section or physical interpretation is
asserted or computed.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\gamma\ge0$, let
$C:=-\Delta-\gamma/|\cdot|$ on $D(C)=W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ be the
self-adjoint operator of [[thm-nrqm-coulomb-infinitesimal-kinetic-bound]] (c) when $\gamma>0$, and the free Fourier multiplier when $\gamma=0$,
and let $U$ be the unitary of
[[thm-nrqm-coulomb-angular-radial-unitary-reduction]] from $L^2(\mathbb R^3)$
onto $K=\bigoplus_{(l,m)}L^2\bigl((0,\infty),dr\bigr)$, with coefficients
$u_{lm}=r\,c_{lm}$. For $l\ge0$ let $V_l$ be the closure of
$C_c^\infty((0,\infty);\mathbb C)$ in $L^2(0,\infty;\mathbb C)$ for the norm
$$\|u\|_{V_l}^2:=\int_0^\infty\Bigl(\Bigl|u'(r)-\frac{u(r)}{r}\Bigr|^2+\frac{l(l+1)}{r^2}|u(r)|^2+|u(r)|^2\Bigr)dr,$$
realized as the space of $u\in L^2$ with $u'-\frac ur\in L^2$ and
$\int|u|^2/r^2<\infty$ in the distributional sense
([[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]],
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), and define
$$a_l(u,v):=\int_0^\infty\Bigl[\overline{\Bigl(v'(r)-\frac{v(r)}{r}\Bigr)}\Bigl(u'(r)-\frac{u(r)}{r}\Bigr)+\frac{l(l+1)}{r^2}u(r)\overline{v(r)}-\frac{\gamma}{r}u(r)\overline{v(r)}\Bigr]dr .$$
Then:

(a) $V_l$ is a dense linear subspace of $L^2(0,\infty)$ that is a Hilbert space for $\|\cdot\|_{V_l}$, the inclusion $V_l\hookrightarrow L^2(0,\infty)$ is continuous, and $a_l$ is a bounded symmetric sesquilinear form on $V_l$ that is closed and semibounded below;

(b) the operator $A_l$ defined by
$$D(A_l):=\Bigl\{u\in V_l:\exists\,f\in L^2(0,\infty)\ \text{with}\ a_l(u,v)=\langle f,v\rangle\ \forall v\in V_l\Bigr\},\qquad A_lu:=f,$$
is well defined, self-adjoint and bounded below; $D(A_l)$ is dense in $V_l$ in the norm $\|\cdot\|_{V_l}$ and $a_l(u,u)=\langle A_lu,u\rangle$ for $u\in D(A_l)$;

(c) for every $u\in D(A_l)$ the distributional identity $-u''+\bigl(l(l+1)/r^2-\gamma/r\bigr)u=A_lu$ holds on $(0,\infty)$; consequently $u\in H^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(0,\infty)$, $u$ is of class $C^1$ with $u'$ locally absolutely continuous, and the identity holds pointwise almost everywhere on $(0,\infty)$; if moreover $A_lu=Eu$ for some constant $E\in\mathbb C$ (in particular if $u$ is an eigenfunction of $A_l$), then $u$ is of class $C^2$ on $(0,\infty)$ and the differential equation holds pointwise there;

(d) *block identity.* For $\psi\in L^2(\mathbb R^3)$ with $U\psi=(u_{lm})$ one has $\psi\in D(C)$ if and only if $u_{lm}\in D(A_l)$ for every $(l,m)$ and $\sum_{l,m}\bigl(\|u_{lm}\|^2+\|A_lu_{lm}\|^2\bigr)<\infty$; then $U(C\psi)=(A_lu_{lm})_{l,m}$. Equivalently $UCU^*=\bigoplus_{(l,m)}A_l$ on $K$;

(e) *eigenfunction transport.* If $u\in D(A_l)$ and $A_lu=Eu$ for some $E\in\mathbb R$, then the function $\psi(x):=u(r)Y_{l0}(\Omega)/r$ (with $x=r\Omega$) lies in $H^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$, satisfies $C\psi=E\psi$, and $r\mapsto u(r)/r$ is bounded on $(0,1]$; moreover $\psi$ is bounded and continuous on $\mathbb R^3$.

No endpoint boundary condition is imposed by hand: the domain $D(A_l)$ is the
form-domain realization transported from $D(C)=H^2(\mathbb R^3)$, and no
physical interpretation of $A_l$, $C$, $U$ or $\gamma$ is asserted.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p<\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then the compactly supported smooth
functions $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ are dense in
$W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$: for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ with
$$\|\varphi-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)}<\delta.$$
No such norm-density assertion is made for $p=\infty$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), let $d\ge1$ and work on $H=L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ ([[def-hilbert-space]]).

(a) For a real measurable finite-valued function $a:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ define $M_af:=af$ on $D(M_a):=\{f\in H: af\in H\}$. Then $M_a$ is a densely defined self-adjoint operator on $H$ ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]).

(b) Let $c>0$, $b\in\mathbb R$, and let $\mathcal F_2$ be the unitary Plancherel transform with the convention $\widehat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}dx$ on $L^1$ ([[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]], [[thm-plancherel]]). Define

$$H_0:=\mathcal F_2^*\,M_{c|\xi|^2+b}\,\mathcal F_2,\qquad D(H_0):=\{f\in H:|\xi|^2\mathcal F_2f\in H\}.$$

Then $H_0$ is self-adjoint, $D(H_0)$ coincides with the Sobolev space $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ as a set (with equivalent norms, [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[thm-fourier-characterisation-of-integer-order-hilbert-sobolev-spaces]]), $H_0\ge b$ in the quadratic-form sense, and for every Schwartz function $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, $H_0f=-(c/4\pi^2)\Delta f+bf$.

(c) If $V:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ is measurable with $\|V\|_\infty<\infty$ and $H:=H_0+M_V$ with domain $D(H_0)$, then $H$ is self-adjoint on $D(H_0)$, is bounded below, and the assignment $t\mapsto e^{itH}$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group whose generator is $iH$: the limit $\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t(e^{itH}\psi-\psi)$ exists exactly for $\psi\in D(H)$ and equals $iH\psi$ ([[lem-self-adjoint-operator-generates-a-strongly-continuous-unitary-group]]).

(d) *Scope*: the argument uses only boundedness and measurability of $V$; it proves nothing for $V\propto-1/|x|$, $V\propto|x|^2$ or the delta interaction, does not identify $H_0$ with any measured free-particle Hamiltonian, and asserts no physical interpretation.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\gamma\ge0$, $l\ge0$,
let $A_l$ be the radial operator of
[[thm-nrqm-coulomb-transported-radial-endpoint-realization]] with spectral
measure $E_{A_l}$ and form domain $V_l$, and for $E>0$ let
$\varphi_l(\sqrt E,\cdot)$ and $\rho_l(E)=\frac{\sqrt E}{\pi|W_l(\sqrt E)|^2}$
be as in [[thm-nrqm-coulomb-continuum-spectral-density]]. Define, for $g$ in
the dense subspace $C_c$ of compactly supported square-integrable functions,
$$(T_lg)(E):=\sqrt{\rho_l(E)}\int_0^\infty\varphi_l(\sqrt E,r)g(r)\,dr\qquad(E>0).$$
Then:

(a) $T_lg\in L^2((0,\infty),dE)$ and $\|T_lg\|^2=\langle E_{A_l}((0,\infty))g,g\rangle$; consequently $T_l$ extends uniquely to a linear isometry
$$\widehat T_l:E_{A_l}((0,\infty))L^2(0,\infty)\longrightarrow L^2((0,\infty),dE)$$
of the positive spectral subspace of $A_l$ into $L^2((0,\infty),dE)$;

(b) $\widehat T_l$ is onto, hence unitary; equivalently the range of $\widehat T_l$ is all of $L^2((0,\infty),dE)$ and the adjoint $\widehat T_l^*$ is an isometry inverse to $\widehat T_l$;

(c) $\widehat T_lA_l\widehat T_l^*$ is multiplication by the independent variable on the domain $\{h\in L^2((0,\infty),dE):\int E^2|h(E)|^2dE<\infty\}$, and $\widehat T_lh(A_l)\widehat T_l^*$ is multiplication by $h$ for every bounded Borel function $h$;

(d) *complete Coulomb spectral resolution.* If $\gamma>0$, the operator $C=-\Delta-\gamma/|\cdot|$ on $H^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ is unitarily equivalent to the diagonal operator
$$\bigoplus_{(l,m)}\Bigl[\Bigl(\bigoplus_{n\ge l+1}\mathbb C\Bigr)\oplus L^2((0,\infty),dE)\Bigr]$$
with the constant $-\gamma^2/(4n^2)$ on the $(n,l,m)$-copy of $\mathbb C$ and multiplication by $E$ on each continuum copy; equivalently there is a unitary $V$ from $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ onto the displayed direct sum with $VCV^*$ equal to that diagonal operator, and the negative part of the spectrum is exhausted by the bound states of [[thm-nrqm-coulomb-negative-subspace-completeness-and-degeneracy]] while the positive part is purely absolutely continuous. If $\gamma=0$, the representation is $\bigoplus_{(l,m)}L^2((0,\infty),dE)$ with multiplication by $E$ and no discrete copies, because the free Fourier multiplier has no nonpositive spectral projection.

The transform is a mathematical spectral representation of $A_l$ and $C$; no
scattering amplitude, phase shift or physical interpretation is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\gamma>0$ and let
$C=-\Delta-\gamma/|\cdot|$ on $D(C)=H^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ be the
self-adjoint operator of [[thm-nrqm-coulomb-infinitesimal-kinetic-bound]] with
essential spectrum $[0,\infty)$. For $n\ge1$, $0\le l\le n-1$ and
$-l\le m\le l$ let $u_{nl}$ be the regular solution of
[[thm-nrqm-coulomb-kummer-recurrence-and-termination]] at $k=\gamma/(2n)$
(the polynomial-exponential solution, unique up to a nonzero scalar), and put
$$\psi_{nlm}(x):=\frac{u_{nl}(r)}{r}Y_{lm}(\Omega)\qquad(x=r\Omega).$$
Then:

(a) each $\psi_{nlm}$ lies in $D(C)$ and $C\psi_{nlm}=-\frac{\gamma^2}{4n^2}\psi_{nlm}$; the vectors $\psi_{nlm}$ with distinct labels are pairwise orthogonal, and for fixed $n$ the eigenspace of $C$ at $-\gamma^2/(4n^2)$ is exactly their span; it has dimension $\sum_{l=0}^{n-1}(2l+1)=n^2$;

(b) after normalization, the family $(\psi_{nlm}/\|u_{nl}\|_2)_{n\ge1,0\le l\le n-1,-l\le m\le l}$ is a complete orthonormal family of the negative spectral subspace $E_C((-\infty,0))L^2(\mathbb R^3)$;

(c) the family is not complete in $L^2(\mathbb R^3)$: the nonnegative spectral subspace $E_C([0,\infty))L^2(\mathbb R^3)$ is nonzero (indeed infinite dimensional), so the bound states alone do not span $L^2$.

All claims concern the mathematical spectral decomposition of $C$; no physical
interpretation is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a
complex Hilbert space, let $A:D(A)\subset H\to H$ be a densely defined
self-adjoint operator with spectral projection valued measure $E$ on the Borel
$\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$
([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]],
[[def-projection-valued-measure]]), and let $c>0$. Write $cA$ for the operator
with $D(cA):=D(A)$ and $(cA)x:=c\,(Ax)$, and for $m_{c}:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$,
$m_{c}(\lambda):=c\lambda$, define
$$F(B):=E\bigl(m_{c}^{-1}(B)\bigr)=E\bigl(c^{-1}B\bigr)\qquad(B\subseteq\mathbb R\ \text{Borel}).$$
Then:

(a) $F$ is a regular projection valued measure on the Borel sets of
$\mathbb R$;

(b) for every bounded Borel $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ the bounded integrals
satisfy $\Phi_{F}(f)=\Phi_{E}(f\circ m_{c})$, and the operator
$\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dF(\lambda)$ of the spectral theorem equals $cA$ with
domain $D(A)$;

(c) consequently $F$ is the spectral projection valued measure $E_{cA}$ of
$cA$: for every Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R$,
$$E_{cA}(B)=E\bigl(c^{-1}B\bigr);$$in particular the negative spectral subspaces agree,$$E_{cA}\bigl((-\infty,0)\bigr)H=E\bigl((-\infty,0)\bigr)H .$$

The assertion transfers the spectral measure along positive scaling of the
operator. It asserts no spectral type of a particular operator, no multiplicity
statement and no physical interpretation; $c<0$ is not covered, and no
statement is made about unbounded Borel functions of $cA$ beyond the identity
functional calculus stated in (b).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

derivations.claim: [The coordinate map] In the three coordinates the matrix of $\Phi$ relative to the splitting $(x_1,x_2)\mapsto(R,r)$ is block diagonal with the $2\times2$ block $\begin{pmatrix}m_1/M&m_2/M\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$ repeated three times; its determinant is $-m_2/M-m_1/M=-1$, so $|\det\Phi|=1$ and $\Phi$ is invertible with the displayed inverse. By the linear change-of-variables theorem the pullback $U_\Phi f=f\circ\Phi^{-1}$ is unitary on $L^2(\mathbb R^6;\mathbb C)$, since it preserves the integral of $|f|^2$; this is (a).

[Kinetic separation on Schwartz functions] Let $f$ be Schwartz. The chain rule gives $\partial_{x_1,j}=\frac{m_1}{M}\partial_{R_j}+\partial_{r_j}$ and $\partial_{x_2,j}=\frac{m_2}{M}\partial_{R_j}-\partial_{r_j}$, hence $\Delta_{x_1}=\frac{m_1^2}{M^2}\Delta_R+2\frac{m_1}{M}\partial_R\cdot\partial_r+\Delta_r$ and $\Delta_{x_2}=\frac{m_2^2}{M^2}\Delta_R-2\frac{m_2}{M}\partial_R\cdot\partial_r+\Delta_r$. Multiplying by $\frac{\hbar^2}{2m_i}$ and summing, the mixed terms cancel because $\frac{m_1}{M}\cdot\frac1{m_1}-\frac{m_2}{M}\cdot\frac1{m_2}=0$, while the $\Delta_R$ coefficient is $-\frac{\hbar^2}{2M}$ and the $\Delta_r$ coefficient is $-\frac{\hbar^2}{2}\bigl(\frac1{m_1}+\frac1{m_2}\bigr)=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2\mu}$; this is the displayed identity of (b) at the level of Schwartz functions.

[The kinetic operators agree as self-adjoint operators] Let $K$ denote the self-adjoint operator on $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^6)$ given by $-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m_1}\Delta_{x_1}-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m_2}\Delta_{x_2}$ (existence by [F2], applied to the Fourier multiplier $4\pi^2(\frac{\hbar^2}{2m_1}|\xi_1|^2+\frac{\hbar^2}{2m_2}|\xi_2|^2)$, which is comparable to $|\xi|^2$), and let $K'$ be the self-adjoint operator on $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^6)$ given by $-\frac{\hbar^2}{2M}\Delta_R-\frac{\hbar^2}{2\mu}\Delta_r$. Both act on Schwartz functions, a common core of $W^{2,2}$-type Fourier-multiplier operators, and step 2.1 shows $U_\Phi KU_\Phi^{-1}f=K'f$ for Schwartz $f$; since $U_\Phi KU_\Phi^{-1}$ and $K'$ are self-adjoint operators agreeing on a common core, they are equal, and $U_\Phi(D(K))=D(K')=H^2(\mathbb R^6;\mathbb C)$. This completes (b).

[Norm lift and two-body self-adjointness] Under $U_\Phi$, the original multiplier $-\kappa/|x_1-x_2|$ becomes $-\kappa/|r|$. First let $w\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R_R^3\times\mathbb R_r^3)$. For each $R$, [F4] gives $\|w(R,\cdot)/|r|\|_{L_r^2}\le\eta\|\Delta_rw(R,\cdot)\|_{L_r^2}+\eta^{-1}\|w(R,\cdot)\|_{L_r^2}$. Taking $L_R^2$ norms and the triangle inequality, with [F8], yields $\|w/|r|\|_2\le\eta\|\Delta_rw\|_2+\eta^{-1}\|w\|_2$. Approximate arbitrary $w\in H^2(\mathbb R^6)$ in its Sobolev norm by [F8]. Applying this estimate to differences makes the quotients Cauchy in $L^2$; closedness of multiplication identifies their limit with $w/|r|$, so the estimate holds on all of $H^2$. The Fourier symbols of $-\Delta_r$ and $K'=-(\hbar^2/(2M))\Delta_R-(\hbar^2/(2\mu))\Delta_r$ are simultaneous nonnegative multipliers $4\pi^2|\xi_r|^2$ and $4\pi^2(\hbar^2|\xi_R|^2/(2M)+\hbar^2|\xi_r|^2/(2\mu))$; their pointwise domination gives $\|\Delta_rw\|_2\le(2\mu/\hbar^2)\|K'w\|_2$ by Plancherel. Therefore $\|\kappa w/|r|\|_2\le(2\kappa\mu\eta/\hbar^2)\|K'w\|_2+(\kappa/\eta)\|w\|_2$, an arbitrarily small operator relative bound. Kato–Rellich [F3] makes $K'-\kappa/|r|$ self-adjoint on $H^2$. Conjugating back gives exactly $H_2=U_\Phi^{-1}(K'-\kappa/|r|)U_\Phi$, self-adjoint on $H^2$; the separated differential expression, under [F6], is $T_R\otimes I+I\otimes C_\mu$. This denotes the self-adjoint commuting spectral sum: choose $c$ with $C_\mu+c\ge0$. In its joint product representation the nonnegative sum has domain equal to the intersection of the two factor domains, because each nonnegative summand is bounded pointwise by their sum. The relative norm bound just proved makes the $C_\mu$ graph norm equivalent to the relative Laplacian graph norm; Fourier comparison of the two nonnegative kinetic weights identifies that intersection with $H^2(\mathbb R^6)$. Thus its graph closure is the same Kato–Rellich operator. This proves (c) with an actual fiber-norm lift and no form-to-norm inference.

[Full spectrum and no eigenvalue by the product representation] By step 4.1 the transformed operator is $T_R\otimes I+I\otimes C_\mu$. Put $\gamma:=2\mu\kappa/\hbar^2>0$ and $c:=\hbar^2/(2\mu)>0$, so $C_\mu=cC_\gamma$ on their common domain $H^2(\mathbb R^3)$. Under $V_\gamma$ of [F9], this is the diagonal operator with scaled bound values $c(-\gamma^2/(4n^2))=-\mu\kappa^2/(2\hbar^2n^2)$ and continuum multiplier $c\lambda$. The PVM transfer in [F9] gives, on a continuum copy, $E_{C_\mu}(B)=M_{\mathbf1_{c^{-1}B}(\lambda)}$ in this representation. Define $(D_ch)(E):=c^{-1/2}h(E/c)$ on each continuum copy, with inverse $(D_c^{-1}g)(\lambda)=c^{1/2}g(c\lambda)$. Changing variables $E=c\lambda$ gives $\int_0^\infty|D_ch(E)|^2dE=\int_0^\infty|h(\lambda)|^2d\lambda$, so $D_c$ is onto unitary. The same substitution gives $\int_0^\infty E^2|D_ch(E)|^2dE=c^2\int_0^\infty\lambda^2|h(\lambda)|^2d\lambda$; hence it maps the exact maximal domain of $cM_\lambda$ onto that of $M_E$ and satisfies $D_c(cM_\lambda)D_c^{-1}=M_E$. On indicators it gives $D_cM_{\mathbf1_{c^{-1}B}(\lambda)}D_c^{-1}=M_{\mathbf1_B(E)}$, explicitly transporting the continuum PVM. The direct sum of the identity on every bound copy and $D_c$ on every continuum copy is onto unitary: its norm identity and inverse hold in each coordinate and therefore in the countable square sum. Composing it with $V_\gamma$ gives the full relative spectral resolution of $C_\mu$, including its diagonal domain and no zero eigenchannel. Apply this unitary and the $2\pi$-normalized center Fourier transform to the tensor decomposition, using [F6] and Plancherel. The absence of nonnegative relative eigenvalues in [F7] agrees with that resolution. The operator becomes the countable sum of real multiplication operators: on each relative bound copy its multiplier is $c_R(\xi)+E_n$, where $c_R(\xi)=4\pi^2\hbar^2|\xi|^2/(2M)$ and $E_n=-\mu\kappa^2/(2\hbar^2n^2)$; on each continuum copy it is $c_R(\xi)+E'$ for $E'>0$. These multipliers are all at least $E_1$, so the operator is bounded below by $E_1$. For every $E\ge E_1$ choose $\xi_0$ with $c_R(\xi_0)=E-E_1$ and normalized smooth Fourier profiles supported in shrinking balls around $\xi_0$. Their inverse transforms $\varphi_\delta$ are Schwartz, and $\|(T_R-(E-E_1))\varphi_\delta\|\to0$ by continuity of $c_R$. The correctly ordered vectors $\varphi_\delta\otimes u_1$ have norm one and belong to the operator domain, with residual $(T_R-(E-E_1))\varphi_\delta\otimes u_1$ tending to zero; a bounded resolvent at $E$ would contradict this, so $E\in\sigma(H_2)$. Hence $\sigma(H_2)=[E_1,\infty)$. For an eigenvalue equation at any real $E$, each bound-component Fourier class must be supported on $\{\xi:c_R(\xi)=E-E_n\}$, a sphere, a point or the empty set, all Lebesgue-null; each continuum component must be supported on $\{(\xi,E'):E'=E-c_R(\xi)\}$, which has zero product measure by Tonelli since every $E'$ section is a singleton. The countable spectral sum therefore has no nonzero eigenvector. All spectral points, including the negative interval, are continuous spectrum because the operator is self-adjoint. Every $E_n$ is the lower edge of its relative bound-channel band $[E_n,\infty)$, a threshold without a total eigenvector. This proves (d) with all masses and couplings retained.

[Maximal directional momentum and no eigenvector] Under the $2\pi$-normalized Plancherel transform in $R$, $P_{R,j}$ is the real multiplier $2\pi\hbar\xi_j$ with maximal domain $\{g:\xi_j\widehat g\in L^2\}$. The weak-derivative Fourier identity identifies this with the domain stated in (e); [F2] and the real-multiplier supplier make it self-adjoint. The full $H^1$ space is a common core for the three operators, not their maximal domain: truncate each Fourier class to bounded balls, then approximate in the weighted norm $(1+\xi_j^2)^{1/2}$ by smooth compactly supported Fourier functions, whose inverse transforms are Schwartz and belong to $H^1$. If $P_{R,j}g=\lambda g$, then $(2\pi\hbar\xi_j-\lambda)\widehat g=0$ a.e., so $\widehat g$ is supported on the hyperplane $\xi_j=\lambda/(2\pi\hbar)$, a Lebesgue-null set by Tonelli [F8]; thus $g=0$ by Plancherel. The same conclusion on the tensor product follows by Tonelli on the remaining relative variables and the Euclidean identification [F6]. This proves (e), and the no-eigenvalue conclusion for $H_2$ in step 5.1 also excludes any simultaneous energy/momentum eigenvector.
[Conclusion] Clauses (a), (b), (c), (d), (e) are steps 1.1, 2.1 and 3.1, 4.1, 5.1, and 6.1.
