derivations.claim: [Endpoint and form membership] Fix $z=k^2$ with $\operatorname{Im}k>0$ in the Jost construction domain; its positive real part makes $z$ nonreal. A function agreeing with a constant multiple of $\varphi_l$ near zero and a constant multiple of $f_l$ near infinity and lying in $H^2$ on intervening compact intervals has $u,u',u/r\in L^2$ and trace zero at zero by [F2]. It belongs to $V_l$: a cutoff vanishing below $\delta$ and equal to one above $2\delta$ adds derivative squared norm at most $C\int_0^{2\delta}|u|^2/r^2\to0$; a cutoff at infinity adds derivative squared norm at most $CR^{-2}\int_R^{2R}|u|^2\to0$. The tails of all other norm terms vanish by integrability, and the resulting compact $H^1$ functions can be smoothed within the open half-line. This verifies actual form membership including $l=0$ and $\gamma=0$.

[Radial form proof of zero exclusion] Define $S_su(r)=e^{s/2}u(e^sr)$ for real $s$. Change of variables gives unitarity on $L^2$, preservation of $V_l$, and on the smooth form core the exact identity $a_l(S_su,v)=e^{2s}a_l(u,S_{-s}v)+\gamma(e^{2s}-e^s)\langle S_s(u/r),v\rangle$. Kinetic and angular terms scale by $e^{2s}$ and the Coulomb term by $e^s$. Continuity extends the identity to all $u,v\in V_l$, since $u/r\in L^2$. If $u\in D(A_l)$ and $A_lu=0$, the form criterion gives $S_su\in D(A_l)$ and $A_lS_su=\gamma(e^{2s}-e^s)S_s(u/r)$. Self-adjointness yields $0=\langle A_lS_su,u\rangle=\gamma(e^{2s}-e^s)\langle S_s(u/r),u\rangle$. For $\gamma>0$ and $s\ne0$ divide by the nonzero coefficient. Strong continuity $S_sh\to h$ follows first for compact continuous $h$ by dominated convergence and then by density and unitarity for all $h\in L^2$. Letting $s\to0$ gives $\int|u|^2/r=0$, hence $u=0$. For $\gamma=0$, $0=\langle A_lu,u\rangle=\|u'-u/r\|_2^2+l(l+1)\|u/r\|_2^2$; the identity $\|u'-u/r\|_2=\|u'\|_2$ extends from the form core to $V_l$, so $u'=0$ and its $L^2$ constant representative is zero. No unbounded dilation generator is differentiated.

[Compact weighted form embedding] The map $K:V_l\to L^2(0,\infty)$, $Ku=u/\sqrt r$, is compact on bounded $H_0^1$ sets. To prove this directly, for $\|u\|_2,\|u'\|_2\le C$ use $\int_0^\delta|u|^2/r\le\delta\|u/r\|_2^2\le4\delta C^2$ and $\int_R^\infty|u|^2/r\le C^2/R$. On $[\delta,R]$, partition into finitely many equal cells of length at most $h$ and replace $u$ by its average on each cell. The absolute continuity formula and Cauchy–Schwarz give $\int_I|u-u_I|^2\le h^2\int_I|u'|^2$ on each cell $I$, so multiplication by $1/\sqrt r$ gives total middle error at most $h^2C^2/\delta$. The resulting functions lie in a fixed finite-dimensional span of cell indicators divided by $\sqrt r$, with bounded coefficients. Choosing $\delta,R,h$ makes the error arbitrarily small, so the image has finite nets of every radius and is relatively compact in complete $L^2$. This explicit finite-rank approximation works for real $l\ge0$ as well as the angular integer labels.

[Nonreal Wronskian] If $W_l(k)=0$, regular-IVP uniqueness makes $\varphi_l$ and $f_l$ proportional, giving a nonzero common solution $u$. Step 1.1 puts $u$ in $V_l$. Integration by parts against compact smooth $v$ gives $a_l(u,v)=z\langle u,v\rangle$, since the derivative form equals $\int u'\overline{v'}$ by cancellation of the derivative of $u\overline v/r$. Form continuity extends this to every $v\in V_l$. The exact criterion [F1] gives $u\in D(A_l)$ and $A_lu=zu$, contradicting self-adjointness. Thus the nonreal Wronskian is nonzero.

[Finite negative spectral bands] Assume $\gamma>0$, put $M=2\gamma^2+1$, and fix $\varepsilon>0$. The range $H_\varepsilon=E_{A_l}([-M,-\varepsilon])L^2$ lies in $D(A_l)$ by bounded energy support; for $u\in H_\varepsilon$ the PVM gives $a_l(u,u)\le-\varepsilon\|u\|^2$. The lower bound [F5] gives $\|u'\|_2^2\le4\gamma^2\|u\|_2^2$, so the unit ball of $H_\varepsilon$ is $H_0^1$-bounded. If this spectral range were infinite-dimensional, AC allows choosing an orthonormal sequence $u_j$ in it (successively choose a unit vector orthogonal to the preceding finite span). For $v=u_j-u_i$, nonnegativity of the kinetic and angular terms and the negative-band bound give $\gamma\|Kv\|_2^2\ge\varepsilon\|v\|_2^2=2\varepsilon$. Thus the images $Ku_j$ are separated by a fixed positive distance, contradicting the finite nets in step 1.3. Hence every negative band has finite-dimensional spectral range. This orthonormal-sequence selection uses the retained AC assumption; the proof does not claim a CC-only recursive choice argument.

[Green sign, derivative jump and actual inverse] Write $\varphi=\varphi_l(k,\cdot)$, $f=f_l(k,\cdot)$, $W=W_l(k)$. For $g$ supported in $[r_1,r_2]\subset(0,\infty)$ let $I(r)=\int_0^r\varphi(s)g(s)ds$, $J(r)=\int_r^\infty f(s)g(s)ds$, and $u=-(fI+\varphi J)/W$. The integrals are absolutely continuous; cross terms cancel in $u'=-(f'I+\varphi'J)/W$, and $u''=-(f''I+\varphi''J)/W-g$. Therefore $-u''+(q_l-z)u=g$ almost everywhere. Below $r_1$ and above $r_2$, $u$ is respectively a constant multiple of $\varphi$ and of $f$, so step 1.1 gives $u\in V_l$. Integration by parts against compact tests and form continuity give $a_l(u,v)=\langle zu+g,v\rangle$ for every $v\in V_l$. Thus $u\in D(A_l)$ and $u=(A_l-z)^{-1}g$. The kernel $G=-\varphi(r_<)f(r_>)/W$ is continuous and its derivative jump is $-[\varphi(s)f'(s)-\varphi'(s)f(s)]/W=-1$, giving $(L_l-z)G=\delta_s$ distributionally. The stated inverse norm estimate is [F1].

[Negative scalar measures are countably atomic] Each band projection in step 2.2 has finite rank $N$. Choose a finite orthonormal basis $e_1,\ldots,e_N$ for its range and define $
u=\sum_j\mu_{e_j}$, supported in the band. Its support has at most $N$ points: otherwise $N+1$ distinct support points admit disjoint open neighborhoods of positive $
u$ mass, hence $N+1$ nonzero mutually orthogonal spectral projection ranges inside this $N$-dimensional space. The complement of this support is the union of the rational open intervals of zero $
u$ mass, so it has zero $
u$ mass by countable subadditivity. Every scalar measure of a vector in the band is likewise supported on this finite set, since $
u(B)=0$ makes $E(B)$ annihilate the basis and hence the entire band range. Exhausting negative energies by $[-M,-1/n]$ shows every radial negative scalar measure is supported on one countable union of finite sets. The lower bound [F5] excludes energies below $-M$. For $\gamma=0$, the form is nonnegative and the negative projection is zero. This proves the negative pure-point fact locally for the whole stated real $l\ge0$ range.

[Boundary algebra for complex sources] For real $k>0$, $\operatorname{Im}(\overline fW)=\varphi\operatorname{Im}(\overline ff')=k\varphi$. Since $-f/W=-f\overline W/|W|^2$, conjugating $\overline fW$ gives $\operatorname{Im}(-f/W)=k\varphi/|W|^2$, proving (b). For a complex source the kernel symmetry $G(r,s)=G(s,r)$ matters: the adjoint kernel on the compact support is $\overline{G(s,r)}=\overline{G(r,s)}$, so $(R-R^*)/(2i)$ has kernel $\operatorname{Im}G$. Consequently Fubini gives $\operatorname{Im}\langle R(k^2+i0)g,g\rangle=k|\int\varphi_l(k,r)g(r)dr|^2/|W_l(k)|^2$. This does not incorrectly distribute imaginary parts across complex source products.

[Uniform compact-source limit] Fix $0<a<b$ and compact source support $J\subset(0,\infty)$. Choose $k_{\min}<\sqrt a$. The set of first-quadrant roots $\{\sqrt{E+i\varepsilon}:E\in[a,b],0\le\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_0\}$ is compact inside the Jost parameter domain. The jointly continuous $\varphi,f,\varphi',f'$ give continuous $W$ computed at any fixed radial point. Its real-axis modulus has a positive minimum on $[\sqrt a,\sqrt b]$, hence a common positive lower bound for sufficiently small $\varepsilon_0$. Uniform continuity therefore gives uniform convergence of $G(E+i\varepsilon;r,s)$ to its boundary value for $E\in[a,b]$ and $r,s\in J$. Since $\|g\|_1\le |J|^{1/2}\|g\|_2$, the paired error is at most the supremum kernel error times $\|g\|_1^2$. Pairings converge uniformly and step 4.1 gives their imaginary parts. No global limiting-absorption norm is assumed.

[Poisson approximation from the PVM] For continuous $h$ compactly supported in $(0,\infty)$, extended by zero to $\mathbb R$, [F3] and Fubini give $\pi^{-1}\int h(E)\operatorname{Im}\langle(A_l-E-i\varepsilon)^{-1}g,g\rangle dE=\int(P_\varepsilon*h)(\lambda)d\mu_g(\lambda)$, where $P_\varepsilon(t)=\varepsilon/[\pi(t^2+\varepsilon^2)]$. Absolute integrability follows from $\int P_\varepsilon=1$ and finite mass $\|g\|^2$. Uniform continuity bounds $|h(x-t)-h(x)|$ by any prescribed $\eta>0$ for $|t|\le\delta$; the remainder is at most $2\|h\|_\infty\int_{|t|>\delta}P_\varepsilon\le4\|h\|_\infty\varepsilon/(\pi\delta)$. Hence $P_\varepsilon*h\to h$ uniformly. For compact-source $g$, step 5.1 computes the other limit, yielding $\int h\,d\mu_g=\int_0^\infty h(E)d_g(E)dE$, with continuous nonnegative $d_g(E)=\rho_l(E)|\int\varphi_l(\sqrt E,r)g(r)dr|^2$.

[Borel density without a regularity prerequisite] For $0<a<b$, continuous $h_n(E)=\min(1,n(E-a)_+,n(b-E)_+)$ increase to $\mathbf1_{(a,b)}$ and vanish outside $[a,b]$. Step 6.1 and dominated convergence give $\mu_g((a,b))=\int_a^b d_g(E)dE$. Every positive singleton has zero mass by shrinking intervals around it and local boundedness of $d_g$. On a fixed compact interval $[c,d]\subset(0,\infty)$, the two finite measures agree on all subintervals, including endpoints. Agreement on every relative Borel set follows by the elementary measure uniqueness argument: agreement sets form a Dynkin class (equal total mass, relative complements, disjoint countable unions), and intervals form an intersection-stable generator. For completeness, let $\mathcal D$ be the smallest Dynkin class containing these intervals and the full compact interval; for a fixed generating interval $I$, the sets $B$ with $I\cap B\in\mathcal D$ form a Dynkin class containing the generators, hence contain $\mathcal D$. Repeating this with any fixed $B\in\mathcal D$ shows that $\mathcal D$ is closed under intersections of its members. A Dynkin class closed under intersections is a sigma algebra by disjointifying countable unions, so it contains the generated Borel sigma algebra. Exhaustion by $[1/n,n]$ proves equality on every positive Borel set. The same exhaustion bounds the total density integral by $\|g\|^2$. This proves density before either Stone's interval formula or an onto transform, without a separate finite-measure regularity assumption.

[Arbitrary vectors] For arbitrary $g\in L^2$, take explicit $g_n=\mathbf1_{[1/n,n]}g\to g$. Projection contraction gives $|\mu_g(B)-\mu_{g_n}(B)|\le(\|g\|+\|g_n\|)\|g-g_n\|$ uniformly over Borel $B$. Every positive Lebesgue-null Borel set has zero $\mu_{g_n}$ mass by step 7.1 and hence zero $\mu_g$ mass. Thus every scalar spectral measure restricted to $(0,\infty)$ is absolutely continuous and every positive atom vanishes. These explicit cutoffs require no additional choice.

[Exact interval Stone formula] PVM representation and Fubini give $\pi^{-1}\int_a^b\operatorname{Im}\langle(A_l-E-i\varepsilon)^{-1}g,g\rangle dE=\int F_\varepsilon(\lambda)d\mu_g(\lambda)$, with $F_\varepsilon(\lambda)=\pi^{-1}[\arctan((b-\lambda)/\varepsilon)-\arctan((a-\lambda)/\varepsilon)]$. It lies in $[0,1]$ and tends to $\mathbf1_{(a,b)}+\tfrac12\mathbf1_{\{a,b\}}$. Dominated convergence and the already proved zero endpoint atoms yield the exact interval formula for every $g$. Step 7.1 gives its compact-source density integral.

[Positive subspace] Put $P_+=E_{A_l}((0,\infty))$. If $g=P_+g$, its entire scalar measure is positive-energy supported and absolutely continuous by step 8.1. Thus this subspace has neither pure-point nor singular-continuous part. Also $P_+g_n\to P_+g$, so positive spectral projections of compact-source vectors span it densely. This permits unprojected compact-source vectors to have negative-energy components.

[Full AC subspace and conclusion] An absolutely continuous scalar measure gives zero mass to the countable negative support from step 3.2 and to $\{0\}$. Hence its vector lies in $P_+L^2$. Step 9.2 proves the reverse inclusion, so the full absolutely continuous subspace equals the positive spectral subspace, establishing corrected clause (d), whose zero exclusion is step 1.2. Clauses (a), (b), (c) follow from the Green inverse, boundary algebra, and PVM Poisson arguments above. The regular normalization and density $\sqrt E/(\pi|W_l(\sqrt E)|^2)$ are unchanged, and neither the onto transform nor any angular transport at noninteger $l$ was assumed.

boundaries.evidence: The null-set intersection defining H_ac includes the empty Borel set, whose PVM projection is zero, so that member imposes no restriction. Compact sources may be g=0 with empty support: F3 gives mu_0=0, and the kernel, density and cutoff arguments in steps 3.1, 6.1-8.1 then vanish. Step 3.2 permits a zero-rank negative band: its basis sum is empty, nu=0, and no nonzero support point is asserted.

The real positive-energy Wronskian is nonzero by the stated Jost interface F2, while step 2.1 proves the nonreal Wronskian nonzero before the Green denominator in step 3.1. Step 1.2 excludes the zero-energy eigenvector separately for gamma>0 and gamma=0. Steps 7.1 and 8.1 exclude all positive atoms, including for the zero source.

The l=0 channel is included by the endpoint/form argument of step 1.1 and the zero-exclusion argument of step 1.2. Step 2.2 allows rank-one negative spectral bands and step 3.2 treats their finite basis/support argument. No special normalization at E=1 is used.

Step 2.1 excludes a nonreal Wronskian zero by self-adjointness; F2 excludes real k>0 zeros. Step 1.2 handles gamma=0 without division by gamma, and step 3.2 gives zero negative projection for that case. Zero-dimensional negative band ranges are allowed in the finite-rank argument.

Step 1.1 establishes form membership at r=0 and radial infinity by cutoffs. Step 1.2 excludes an atom at energy 0. Steps 7.1-8.1 exclude positive atoms before step 9.1 takes the interval Poisson limit, so its half-weight endpoint terms vanish. No uniform density bound at E=0 or E=infinity is asserted.

The Statement retains AC and CC. Step 2.2 uses AC only to select an orthonormal sequence if a negative band were infinite dimensional; step 3.2 uses a finite basis when its dimension is positive. Step 8.1 uses the explicit cutoffs g_n=1_[1/n,n] g and needs no additional selection; zero-rank bands use the empty basis.

For the equality H_ac(A_l)=E_A_l((0,infinity))L2 in clause (d), step 10.1 shows an absolutely continuous scalar measure gives zero mass to the countable negative support of step 3.2 and to {0}, hence the vector lies in the positive subspace.

For the reverse inclusion in clause (d), step 8.1 proves positive-energy restrictions of every scalar measure absolutely continuous; step 9.2 applies this to positive-subspace vectors, whose entire measures are positive-supported, and step 10.1 concludes the equality.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\gamma\ge0$, $l\ge0$,
let $A_l$ be the radial operator of
[[thm-nrqm-coulomb-transported-radial-endpoint-realization]] with spectral
measure $E_{A_l}$, and for $k>0$ let $\varphi_l(k,\cdot)$ and $f_l(k,\cdot)$
be the solutions of [[thm-nrqm-coulomb-jost-volterra-solution]], with
$W_l(k):=W(\varphi_l(k,\cdot),f_l(k,\cdot))\ne0$. Write
$$\rho_l(E):=\frac{\sqrt E}{\pi\,|W_l(\sqrt E)|^2}\qquad(E>0).$$

For $g\in L^2(0,\infty)$ write $\mu_g(B):=\langle E_{A_l}(B)g,g\rangle$
for its finite positive scalar spectral measure, where $B\subseteq\mathbb R$
is Borel ([[def-projection-valued-measure]],
[[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]). A finite
positive Borel measure $\mu$ is *absolutely continuous* with respect to
Lebesgue measure $dE$ if $\mu(N)=0$ for every Borel set $N$ of Lebesgue measure
zero; it is *singular continuous* if it is carried by a Borel Lebesgue-null
set and has no atoms, meaning $\mu(\{E\})=0$ for every $E\in\mathbb R$.
Define the absolutely continuous subspace
$$\mathcal H_{\mathrm{ac}}(A_l):=\{g\in L^2(0,\infty):\mu_g\text{ is absolutely continuous with respect to }dE\}.$$
It is a closed linear subspace because it equals
$\bigcap_{N:\,|N|=0}\ker E_{A_l}(N)$, where the intersection is over Borel
Lebesgue-null sets and $\mu_g(N)=\|E_{A_l}(N)g\|^2$.
For $I=(0,\infty)$, put
$$\mathcal H_{\mathrm{sc}}(A_l;I):=\{g\in E_{A_l}(I)L^2(0,\infty):\mu_g\text{ is singular continuous}\}.$$
The set $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{sc}}(A_l;I)$ is a closed linear subspace:
linear combinations of such vectors have scalar measures supported on the
union of their null carriers and have no atoms, and these two properties pass
to limits of vectors by continuity of the PVM projections. Here $E_{A_l}(I)L^2$ is
*purely absolutely continuous* when it is contained in $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{ac}}(A_l)$,
and “$A_l$ has no singular-continuous spectrum on $I$” means
$\mathcal H_{\mathrm{sc}}(A_l;I)=\{0\}$. Thus each operator spectral-type
phrase in (d) is a statement about the scalar PVM measures, not an additional
pointwise classification of energies.

Then:

(a) *resolvent kernel.* For $z=k^2$ with $\operatorname{Im}k>0$ and $k$ in the domain of the Jost construction, and for every $g\in L^2(0,\infty)$ with compact support, the resolvent is given by
$$((A_l-z)^{-1}g)(r)=\int_0^\infty G_l(r,s)g(s)\,ds,\qquad G_l(r,s):=-\frac{\varphi_l(k,\min(r,s))\,f_l(k,\max(r,s))}{W_l(k)},$$
and $G_l$ solves $(A_l-z)G_l=\delta$ in the sense that $-G''+(l(l+1)/r^2-\gamma/r)G-zG=0$ away from $r=s$ and the derivative of $G$ has the jump $-1$ at $r=s$; moreover $\|(A_l-z)^{-1}\|\le1/|\operatorname{Im}z|$;

(b) *boundary value.* For real $k>0$ one has $\varphi_l(k,\cdot)$ real and, for all $r,s>0$,
$$\operatorname{Im}G_l(k^2+i0;r,s)=\frac{k\,\varphi_l(k,r)\varphi_l(k,s)}{|W_l(k)|^2};$$

(c) *spectral density.* For every $g\in L^2(0,\infty)$ and every $0<a<b$,
$$\langle E_{A_l}((a,b))g,g\rangle=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\frac1\pi\int_a^b\operatorname{Im}\bigl\langle(A_l-E-i\varepsilon)^{-1}g,g\bigr\rangle dE,$$
and if $g$ has compact support then
$$\langle E_{A_l}((a,b))g,g\rangle=\int_a^b\rho_l(E)\Bigl|\int_0^\infty\varphi_l(\sqrt E,r)g(r)\,dr\Bigr|^2dE;$$
consequently for compactly supported $g$ the measure $E_{A_l,g}(B):=\langle E_{A_l}(B)g,g\rangle$ restricted to $(0,\infty)$ is absolutely continuous with density $\rho_l(E)|\int\varphi_l g|^2$;

(d) *absolutely continuous spectrum; no zero eigenvalue.* For every $g\in L^2(0,\infty)$ the measure $E_{A_l,g}$ has no atom in $(0,\infty)$; the positive spectral subspace $E_{A_l}((0,\infty))L^2(0,\infty)$ is purely absolutely continuous and is the closed span of the positive spectral projections of compactly supported functions; it equals the absolutely continuous subspace of $A_l$, and $A_l$ has no singular continuous spectrum on $(0,\infty)$; moreover $0$ is not an eigenvalue of $A_l$.

No scattering phase, normalization of the continuum functions as a unitary
transform, or physical cross-section is asserted; the transform itself is the
subject of the companion item [[thm-nrqm-coulomb-onto-radial-continuum-transform]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\gamma\ge0$, $l\ge0$,
and let $A_l$ be the radial operator of
[[thm-nrqm-coulomb-transported-radial-endpoint-realization]] with form domain
$V_l$. Fix $k_{\min}>0$ and let $K:=\{k\in\mathbb C:\operatorname{Re}k\ge k_{\min},\ \operatorname{Im}k\ge0\}$.
Then:

(a) *regular solution.* With $c_0:=1$, $c_{-1}:=0$ and
$$c_n:=-\frac{\gamma c_{n-1}+k^2c_{n-2}}{n(n+2l+1)}\qquad(n\ge1),$$
the series $\varphi_l(k,r):=r^{l+1}\sum_{n\ge0}c_nr^n$ converges for every $r>0$ and every $k\in\mathbb C$, the function $(k,r)\mapsto\varphi_l(k,r)$ is holomorphic in $k$ and $C^\infty$ in $r>0$, and $\varphi_l$ solves $-u''+\bigl(l(l+1)/r^2-\gamma/r\bigr)u=k^2u$ with $\varphi_l(k,r)/r^{l+1}\to1$ as $r\downarrow0$;

(b) *Jost-type solution.* Put $a:=\gamma/(2k)$, $\theta(r):=kr+a\log r$, $w(r):=e^{i\theta(r)}$, $b:=a^2+l(l+1)+ia$ and consider the integral equation
$$v(r)=1+\int_r^\infty\frac{b}{s^2}\,w(s)^2\Bigl(\int_r^sw(y)^{-2}dy\Bigr)v(s)\,ds .$$
For every $k\in K$ with $k\ne0$ the equation has exactly one bounded solution $v(\cdot;k)$ on $[r_0,\infty)$ for some $r_0>0$ depending on $k$, and $v(r)=1+O(1/r)$, $v'(r)=O(1/r)$; the functions $f_l(k,r):=w(r)v(r)$ and $v$ are continuous on $K$, holomorphic in $k$ for $\operatorname{Im}k>0$, satisfy the radial equation $-\partial_r^2f_l+\bigl(l(l+1)/r^2-\gamma/r\bigr)f_l=k^2f_l$ exactly, and obey the asymptotics
$$f_l=e^{i(kr+a\log r)}(1+O(1/r)),\qquad f_l'=e^{i(kr+a\log r)}[ik+O(1/r)]\qquad(r\to\infty);$$

(c) *Wronskians.* For real $k>0$ one has $W(\overline{f_l},f_l)=2ik$ and $W_l(k):=W(\varphi_l,f_l)\ne0$; consequently every solution of the radial equation on $(0,\infty)$ is $Af_l+B\overline{f_l}$ with $A,B\in\mathbb C$, and $\varphi_l$ is a nonzero complex multiple combination of $f_l,\overline{f_l}$;

(d) *no positive eigenvalue.* For real $k>0$ and $A,B\in\mathbb C$, if $g=Af_l+B\overline{f_l}$ then $\int_R^L|g(r)|^2dr=(|A|^2+|B|^2)[L-R-\gamma\log(L/R)/(2k^2)]+O(1)$ as $L\to\infty$ with $R>r_0$ fixed; hence $g\in L^2(r_0,\infty)$ if and only if $A=B=0$, and $k^2>0$ is not an eigenvalue of $A_l$.

All assertions concern the ordinary differential equation and the operator
$A_l$; no scattering amplitude, cross-section or physical interpretation is
asserted or computed.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $X$ be a normed space, let $D \subseteq X$ be a dense normed subspace, let
$Y$ be a Banach space, and let $T:D\to Y$ be a bounded linear operator. Then
there is a unique bounded linear operator $\widetilde T:X\to Y$ such that

$$\widetilde T|_D = T,$$

and $\|\widetilde T\| = \|T\|$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

- For $0<p<\infty$, define an equivalence relation on $\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ by
  $$f\sim g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f-g\in\mathcal N(\mu),$$
  and write $L^p(\mu)$ for the set of classes $[f]$.
- For $p=\infty$, define the same relation on $L^\infty(\mu)$ and again write
  $L^\infty(\mu)$ for the set of classes.

Thus an element of $L^p(\mu)$ is an almost-everywhere equivalence class of
measurable representatives.

When $1\le p\le\infty$, the displayed set quotient agrees with the usual
quotient-vector-space construction of
[[def-quotient-vector-space-and-canonical-projection]].

For $0<p<1$, the same class notation is used; under its stated choice hypothesis, the later item
[[thm-the-l-p-distance-for-zero-less-p-less-one-is-a-complete-translation-invariant-metric]]
supplies the metric structure rather than a normed-space structure.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on the nonzero
complex Hilbert space $H$. Then there is a unique regular projection valued
measure $E$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ such that
$$
D(T)=\Bigl\{x\in H:\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_x(\lambda)<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad Tx=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE(\lambda)x\quad(x\in D(T)).
$$
Conversely, if $E$ is a regular projection valued measure on $\mathbb R$, then
the operator $\int\lambda\,dE$ with that domain is self-adjoint and its
spectral projection valued measure is $E$ again.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator with spectral
projection valued measure $E$ on $\mathbb R$ acting on a complex Hilbert space $H$
([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]) and let
$f,g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be Borel. Write $u(T)=u(E)$, with the truncation definition below. If $H=\{0\}$, use its unique PVM and unique full-domain operator directly. Then:

1. $f(T)^*=\overline f(T)$;
2. $f(T)g(T)$ has domain $D(g(T))\cap D((fg)(T))$ and equals the restriction of
   $(fg)(T)$ to that domain, and its closure is $(fg)(T)$;
3. on $D(f(T))\cap D(g(T))$ the sum $f(T)+g(T)$ equals the restriction of
   $(f+g)(T)$, and the closure of $f(T)+g(T)$ is $(f+g)(T)$;
4. the spectrum of $f(T)$ is the essential range
   $\{z\in\mathbb C:E(f^{-1}(B_\varepsilon(z)))\ne0$ for every
   $\varepsilon>0\}$ of $f$ with respect to $E$;
5. if $f$ is continuous then that essential range is the closure of
   $f(\sigma(T))$, with the closure redundant when $f(\sigma(T))$ is closed.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on $H$. Then every nonreal number belongs to
$\rho(T)$: $\mathbb C\setminus\mathbb R\subseteq\rho(T)$. More precisely, for
$z=a+ib$ with $a,b\in\mathbb R$, $b\ne0$, and every $x\in D(T)$,
$$\|(T-z)x\|^2=\|(T-a)x\|^2+b^2\|x\|^2 ,$$
and consequently $\|R_T(z)\|\le 1/|\operatorname{Im}z|$. In particular
$\sigma(T)\subseteq\mathbb R$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$. Then every $x\in H$ has a unique decomposition

$$x=m+n,\qquad m\in M,\quad n\in M^\perp ,$$

so that $H=M\oplus M^\perp$ as a direct sum of the subspace $M$ and its orthogonal complement.

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\gamma\ge0$, $l\ge0$,
and let $A_l$ be the radial operator of
[[thm-nrqm-coulomb-transported-radial-endpoint-realization]] with form domain
$V_l$. Fix $k_{\min}>0$ and let $K:=\{k\in\mathbb C:\operatorname{Re}k\ge k_{\min},\ \operatorname{Im}k\ge0\}$.
Then:

(a) *regular solution.* With $c_0:=1$, $c_{-1}:=0$ and
$$c_n:=-\frac{\gamma c_{n-1}+k^2c_{n-2}}{n(n+2l+1)}\qquad(n\ge1),$$
the series $\varphi_l(k,r):=r^{l+1}\sum_{n\ge0}c_nr^n$ converges for every $r>0$ and every $k\in\mathbb C$, the function $(k,r)\mapsto\varphi_l(k,r)$ is holomorphic in $k$ and $C^\infty$ in $r>0$, and $\varphi_l$ solves $-u''+\bigl(l(l+1)/r^2-\gamma/r\bigr)u=k^2u$ with $\varphi_l(k,r)/r^{l+1}\to1$ as $r\downarrow0$;

(b) *Jost-type solution.* Put $a:=\gamma/(2k)$, $\theta(r):=kr+a\log r$, $w(r):=e^{i\theta(r)}$, $b:=a^2+l(l+1)+ia$ and consider the integral equation
$$v(r)=1+\int_r^\infty\frac{b}{s^2}\,w(s)^2\Bigl(\int_r^sw(y)^{-2}dy\Bigr)v(s)\,ds .$$
For every $k\in K$ with $k\ne0$ the equation has exactly one bounded solution $v(\cdot;k)$ on $[r_0,\infty)$ for some $r_0>0$ depending on $k$, and $v(r)=1+O(1/r)$, $v'(r)=O(1/r)$; the functions $f_l(k,r):=w(r)v(r)$ and $v$ are continuous on $K$, holomorphic in $k$ for $\operatorname{Im}k>0$, satisfy the radial equation $-\partial_r^2f_l+\bigl(l(l+1)/r^2-\gamma/r\bigr)f_l=k^2f_l$ exactly, and obey the asymptotics
$$f_l=e^{i(kr+a\log r)}(1+O(1/r)),\qquad f_l'=e^{i(kr+a\log r)}[ik+O(1/r)]\qquad(r\to\infty);$$

(c) *Wronskians.* For real $k>0$ one has $W(\overline{f_l},f_l)=2ik$ and $W_l(k):=W(\varphi_l,f_l)\ne0$; consequently every solution of the radial equation on $(0,\infty)$ is $Af_l+B\overline{f_l}$ with $A,B\in\mathbb C$, and $\varphi_l$ is a nonzero complex multiple combination of $f_l,\overline{f_l}$;

(d) *no positive eigenvalue.* For real $k>0$ and $A,B\in\mathbb C$, if $g=Af_l+B\overline{f_l}$ then $\int_R^L|g(r)|^2dr=(|A|^2+|B|^2)[L-R-\gamma\log(L/R)/(2k^2)]+O(1)$ as $L\to\infty$ with $R>r_0$ fixed; hence $g\in L^2(r_0,\infty)$ if and only if $A=B=0$, and $k^2>0$ is not an eigenvalue of $A_l$.

All assertions concern the ordinary differential equation and the operator
$A_l$; no scattering amplitude, cross-section or physical interpretation is
asserted or computed.

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

derivations.claim: [Isometry on compact sources] For compactly supported $g$, [F1] with $a\downarrow0$, $b\uparrow\infty$ (or the monotone convergence of the positive measures on the increasing intervals $(1/k,k)$) gives $\|T_lg\|^2_{L^2((0,\infty),dE)}=\int_0^\infty\rho_l(E)\bigl|\int\varphi_l(\sqrt E,r)g(r)dr\bigr|^2dE=\langle E_{A_l}((0,\infty))g,g\rangle$; the right side is finite because it is the mass of the finite measure $E_{A_l,g}$ on $(0,\infty)$. This is the isometry of (a) on the dense set $C_c$.

[Extension through the positive projection] Step 1.1 gives $\|T_lg\|\le\|g\|$ on compact sources, so extend $T_l$ first to a contraction $T$ on all $L^2$. Passing to compact-source approximations yields $\|Tg\|^2=\langle P_+g,g\rangle$ for every $g$, where $P_+=E_{A_l}((0,\infty))$. Thus $T(I-P_+)=0$ and $\widehat T=T|_{P_+H}$ is an isometry. Its range is closed because Cauchy sequences in that range pull back to Cauchy sequences in the complete positive subspace. In particular compact-source images are dense in its range, without incorrectly calling $T_l$ isometric on all compact sources.

[Compressed resolvents and the missing norm equality] Write $W=\widehat T:H_+\to K$, $M=\operatorname{ran}W$ and $Q$ for the orthogonal projection onto this closed range. Define $W^*=W^{-1}Q$: uniqueness of orthogonal decomposition gives directly $\langle Wu,v\rangle=\langle u,W^*v\rangle$, $W^*W=I_{H_+}$ and $WW^*=Q$, without invoking another representation theorem. Polarize [F1] on compact sources; the mixed measures are finite, and equality on positive intervals extends to all positive Borel sets by the interval-generated finite-measure uniqueness argument. Integration of bounded simple functions and bounded approximation then gives $\langle M_bTg,Th\rangle=\langle b_+(A_l)g,h\rangle$, where $b_+$ is $b$ on the positive half-line and zero elsewhere. Boundedness extends this identity from compact sources to all $g,h\in H$. Thus $W^*M_bW=b(A_+)$, initially only a compression. For $z=x+iy$, $y\ne0$, put $m_z(E)=(E-z)^{-1}$ and $R_z=(A_+-z)^{-1}$. The identity gives $QM_{m_z}Wu=WR_zu$. Pointwise $\operatorname{Im}m_z=y|m_z|^2$, so $\operatorname{Im}\langle M_{m_z}Wu,Wu\rangle=y\|M_{m_z}Wu\|^2$. Setting $v=R_zu$ and $u=(A_+-z)v$, self-adjointness and the linear-first convention give $\operatorname{Im}\langle R_zu,u\rangle=\operatorname{Im}\langle v,(A_+-z)v\rangle=y\|R_zu\|^2$. The compressed pairing identifies these imaginary parts. Dividing by the nonzero real $y$ proves $\|M_{m_z}Wu\|^2=\|R_zu\|^2=\|WR_zu\|^2=\|QM_{m_z}Wu\|^2$. Pythagoras forces $(I-Q)M_{m_z}Wu=0$. Apply this to both $z$ and $\overline z$, whose multipliers are adjoints: $M$ and $M^\perp$ reduce these multipliers, $Q$ commutes with them, and $M_{m_z}W=WR_z$. This is the required compression-to-reduction proof before any onto claim.

[Resolvent reduction implies indicator reduction] For $0<a<b$ and $\varepsilon>0$, define $p_{\varepsilon,a,b}(E)=\pi^{-1}\int_a^b\varepsilon/[(E-t)^2+\varepsilon^2]dt$. Its multiplier commutes with $Q$: it is the operator-norm Riemann-integral limit of the imaginary parts of $M_{m_{t+i\varepsilon}}$, since $\|M_{m_{t+i\varepsilon}}-M_{m_{s+i\varepsilon}}\|\le|t-s|/\varepsilon^2$. One has $0\le p_{\varepsilon,a,b}\le1$, and these functions tend as $\varepsilon=1/n\downarrow0$ to $\mathbf1_{(a,b)}$ except at the two Lebesgue-null endpoints. Dominated convergence against $|h|^2$ for each $h\in K$ gives strong convergence of the multipliers, so $Q$ commutes with $M_{\mathbf1_{(a,b)}}$. The Borel sets whose multipliers commute with $Q$ form a sigma-algebra: complements use $I-M_{\mathbf1_B}$, intersections use products, and disjoint countable unions use strongly convergent finite sums; disjointification gives arbitrary countable unions. Positive intervals generate the Borel sigma-algebra, so all Borel indicators commute with $Q$. Bounded simple approximation gives all bounded Borel multipliers; completed-measurable sets have the same multiplier as a Borel representative modulo null sets.

[The reducing projection is a scalar indicator] Set $q(E)=e^{-E}>0$ in $K$, $\psi=Qq$ and $a=\psi/q$ using measurable representatives. Commutation gives $Q(bq)=b\psi$ for bounded measurable $b$. For every measurable $B$, contractivity gives $\int_B|\psi|^2\le\int_Bq^2$, hence $|a|\le1$ a.e.; otherwise intersecting $\{|a|>1+1/n\}$ with a bounded positive interval gives a contradiction to this inequality. Vectors $bq$ are dense: for $h\in K$, $h_n=\mathbf1_{\{1/n<E<n,\ |h/q|\le n\}}h$ have that form and converge in $K$ by dominated convergence. Therefore $Q=M_a$ on $K$. Self-adjointness and idempotence force $a=\overline a=a^2$ a.e., testing the multiplier identities on bounded-interval indicators. Thus $Q=M_{\mathbf1_S}$ for a measurable $S$, and $M=L^2(S)$.

[Countable compact tests eliminate the complement] For the explicit family $g_j$ of [F5], each $T_lg_j$ lies in $M=L^2(S)$ and vanishes a.e. on $S^c$. Remove the union of the countably many exceptional null sets. For every remaining $E\in S^c$, positivity of $\rho_l(E)$ gives $\int\varphi_l(\sqrt E,r)g_j(r)dr=0$ for every $j$. On each $(1/k,k)$, $k\ge2$, this is a continuous linear functional by Cauchy-Schwarz and local square integrability of $\varphi_l$. Its vanishing on the fixed dense family implies its vanishing on all of $L^2(1/k,k)$, including $\overline{\varphi_l}\mathbf1_{(1/k,k)}$. Hence $\int_{1/k}^k|\varphi_l|^2=0$. Exhausting $(0,\infty)$ contradicts the nonzero continuous regular solution of [F1]. The remaining part of $S^c$ is therefore empty, so $S^c$ is null, $Q=I_K$, and $W$ is unitary with isometric inverse $W^*$. Only countably many conull sets were intersected. This proves (b).

[Exact bounded and unbounded diagonalization] Steps 3.1, 4.1 and 6.1 give $\widehat T E_{A_l}(B)|_{P_+H}=M_{\mathbf1_B}\widehat T$ for every positive Borel set. Linear combinations and bounded pointwise simple approximation therefore give $\widehat T h(A_l)|_{P_+H}\widehat T^*=M_{h|_{(0,\infty)}}$ for every bounded Borel $h$. This uses the onto-ness of step 6.1 and does not incorrectly pair negative components through $T$. For unbounded energy, spectral truncation and the norm formula give $\int E^2|\widehat T g(E)|^2dE=\int_{(0,\infty)}\lambda^2dE_g(\lambda)$, so the exact generator domain is $\{h:Eh\in L^2(dE)\}$ and $\widehat T A_l|_{P_+H}\widehat T^*=M_E$ there.

[Inverse integral and exact scope of convergence] For $h\in K$ put $h_n=\mathbf1_{(1/n,n)}h$ and $v_n(r)=\int_{1/n}^n\sqrt{\rho_l(E)}\varphi_l(\sqrt E,r)h(E)dE$. The compact parameter bounds of [F5] and Cauchy-Schwarz give $v_n\in L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(0,\infty)$. Fubini for compact-source $g$ gives $\langle Tg,h_n\rangle=\langle g,v_n\rangle$. Since $T=W P_+$ and $W^*h_n\in H_+$, the left side also equals $\langle g,W^*h_n\rangle$. All compact-source tests therefore identify $v_n$ locally a.e. with $W^*h_n$, so $v_n$ represents a global $L^2$ element of $H_+$. Finally $h_n\to h$ in $K$ and $W^*$ is an isometry, giving $W^*h=\lim_{n\to\infty}v_n$ in $L^2(dr)$. This explicitly realizes the inverse without asserting pointwise convergence at infinity. If compact source means bounded support that may approach zero, cutting it off below $1/n$ and using the regular $r^{l+1}$ bound of [F5] extends all compact-energy integral identities by Cauchy-Schwarz and $L^2$ continuity.

[Complete resolution of $C$] By the block identity of [[thm-nrqm-coulomb-transported-radial-endpoint-realization]] and the angular unitary of [[thm-nrqm-coulomb-angular-radial-unitary-reduction]], $C$ is unitarily equivalent to the direct sum over $(l,m)$ of the operators $A_l$, and by the previous items $A_l$ is unitarily equivalent to $M_E$ on $L^2((0,\infty),dE)$ together with the discrete eigenvalues $-\gamma^2/(4n^2)$, $n\ge l+1$, each simple, whose eigenspaces are spanned by the transported regular solutions ([[thm-nrqm-coulomb-negative-subspace-completeness-and-degeneracy]], [[thm-nrqm-coulomb-laguerre-bound-energy-exhaustion]]); the essential spectrum is $[0,\infty)$ and the positive spectrum is purely absolutely continuous by [[thm-nrqm-coulomb-continuum-spectral-density]]. The absence of a zero eigenvector follows from [[thm-nrqm-coulomb-continuum-spectral-density]]. For $\gamma>0$, PVM transport from [F3] through the angular unitary and the exact block identity shows that the normalized global negative eigenfamily restricts to a complete radial negative family in each channel; otherwise placing a missing radial vector in one channel contradicts global completeness. Thus each radial unitary sends $u$ to $((\langle u,u_{nl}/\|u_{nl}\|\rangle)_{n\ge l+1},W P_+u)$, with inverse the $L^2$ bound-family sum plus step 7.2. Assembling these unitaries in the fixed countable channel order gives the stated onto unitary $V$, since orthogonal norm sums give convergence and surjectivity. The exact block domain and step 7.1 identify its diagonal domain with square summability of all energy-multiplied discrete and continuum coordinates. For $\gamma=0$, use the transported free operator: its explicit Fourier multiplier $|p|^2$ has zero projection on $(-\infty,0]$, since $\{p=0\}$ is null. PVM uniqueness and unitary transport in [F3] give $\bigoplus_{l,m}E_{A_l}((-\infty,0])=0$, so every individual nonpositive block projection is zero. Each free radial block is consequently wholly positive, and the same positive transforms assemble a continuum-only unitary. No zero-energy bound copies are introduced.
[Conclusion] Clauses (a), (b), (c), (d) are steps 1.1 and 2.1; 3.1 through 6.1; 7.1; and 8.1. Step 7.2 explicitly realizes the isometric adjoint inverse.

boundaries.reason: No empty family occurs; the range of T_l is characterized as L^2 of a set S that is later shown to have full measure, and the index l >= 0 is nonempty.

boundaries.evidence: The zero-energy boundary is excluded by construction: T_l is defined on the positive spectral subspace E_{A_l}((0, infinity)) L^2, and step 6.1 records the complete resolution of C off the possible kernel at 0, in line with the no-atom result quoted from the spectral-density item.
The identity operator case h = 1 is covered by step 5.1's multiplication identity for every bounded Borel h, and step 1.1 is stated first on compactly supported g, the dense case.

The degenerate possibility that the range misses a set of positive measure is excluded in step 4.1: the projection Q equals multiplication by the indicator of a measurable set S of full measure, so no positive-measure part of L^2((0,infinity), dE) is missed.

The spectral endpoints E -> 0 and E -> infinity are treated set-theoretically: step 4.1 allows exceptions only on null sets, and step 5.1 realizes the multiplication form on the domain {h : int E^2 |h(E)|^2 dE < infinity}; no pointwise claim at E = 0 is made.
Countable Choice and Choice are assumed; step 2.1 extends the isometry from C_c by density and step 3.1 uses the polarization identities on countably many test pairs, as declared in the statement.
Statement (b) is an equivalence and the forward direction "onto implies unitary with the adjoint as inverse isometry" is established by steps 4.1 and 5.1.
The reverse direction "range all of L^2 implies onto, hence unitary" is the same steps read backwards; step 4.1 proves the range is L^2(S) with S of full measure, which is the nontrivial half.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\sigma$ be the polar surface measure on
$S^2$ ([[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]) and let $(Y_{lm})_{l\ge0,\ -l\le m\le l}$ be the
functions of [[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-associated-polynomial-normalization]] ([[def-complex-exponential]]).
Then $(Y_{lm})$ is a complete orthonormal family of the complex Hilbert space $L^2(S^2,\sigma)$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]):
the family is orthonormal, and if $F\in L^2(S^2,\sigma)$ satisfies
$\int_{S^2}F\overline{Y_{lm}}\,d\sigma=0$ for all $l\ge0$ and $-l\le m\le l$, then $F=0$ almost everywhere.
Consequently every $F$ has the expansion
$$F=\sum_{l=0}^\infty\sum_{m=-l}^{l}\langle F,Y_{lm}\rangle Y_{lm},\qquad \|F\|^2=\sum_{l,m}|\langle F,Y_{lm}\rangle|^2,$$
with $\langle F,Y_{lm}\rangle=\int_{S^2}F\overline{Y_{lm}}\,d\sigma$ and finite-subset-net convergence
([[thm-parseval-equivalences-for-a-complete-orthonormal-family]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$S^2:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|=1\}$ and let $\sigma$ be the polar surface measure on $S^2$ of
[[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]], a finite Borel measure ([[def-measure]],
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Let

$$\Phi:(0,\pi)\times(0,2\pi)\to S^2,\qquad \Phi(\theta,\varphi):=(\sin\theta\cos\varphi,\ \sin\theta\sin\varphi,\ \cos\theta),$$

and let $H:=\{(x,y,0)\in\mathbb R^3:x\ge0\}$ denote the closed half-plane, a Lebesgue-null Borel set
([[thm-affine-hyperplanes-and-proper-subspaces-of-rn-are-lebesgue-null]]). Then:

(a) for every Borel function $F:S^2\to[0,+\infty]$,
$$\int_{S^2}F\,d\sigma=\int_{(0,\pi)\times(0,2\pi)}F\bigl(\Phi(\theta,\varphi)\bigr)\,\sin\theta\ d(\theta,\varphi),$$
the right-hand integral being the Lebesgue integral over the open rectangle;

(b) $\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$;

(c) the identity of (a) holds with $F\in L^1(S^2,\sigma;\mathbb C)$ in the sense that $F\circ\Phi$ is Lebesgue
integrable on the rectangle against $\sin\theta\,d(\theta,\varphi)$ and the two integrals agree (real and
imaginary parts, positive and negative parts).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

Assume Countable Choice and let $n\ge1$. For every $u\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ and every multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$,
$$\mathcal F(D^\alpha u)=(2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\mathcal Fu\qquad\text{in }\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n),$$
where $D^\alpha$ is the distributional derivative of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]] and $\mathcal F$ is
the negative-sign $2\pi$-normalized transform. Moreover, if $u=u_f$ and
$D^\alpha u=u_g$ for $L^2$ classes $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb R^n)$ and their regular
distributions, then the unitary Plancherel transforms satisfy
$$\mathcal F_2g(\xi)=(2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\mathcal F_2f(\xi)\qquad\text{for almost every }\xi\in\mathbb R^n.$$
The second assertion compares the Plancherel classes only; it neither asserts
pointwise values of arbitrary representatives nor presupposes any Sobolev-space
notation.

Assume Countable Choice, let $n\ge1$ and $k\in\mathbb N_0$, and use complex
scalars. Write $W^{k,2}=W^{k,2}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ for the weak-derivative
Sobolev space of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], whose classes carry
the weak derivatives $D^\alpha f\in L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ for
$|\alpha|\le k$ and the norm
$$\|f\|_{W^{k,2}}=\Bigl(\sum_{|\alpha|\le k}\|D^\alpha f\|_2^2\Bigr)^{1/2},$$
and let $H^k=H^k(\mathbb R^n)$ be the real-order Bessel-potential completion
of [[def-real-order-bessel-potential-sobolev-space]] with its canonical
embedding $E_k:H^k\to\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$
([[thm-bessel-potential-completions-embed-in-tempered-distributions]]). Let
$u_f\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ denote the regular tempered distribution of
an $L^2$ class $f$. Then:

1. $E_k[H^k]=\{u_f:f\in W^{k,2}\}$, and
   $\Phi(f):=E_k^{-1}(u_f)$ is a bijection
   $\Phi:W^{k,2}\to H^k$. Thus, under the regular-distribution embedding,
   $W^{k,2}$ and $H^k$ are the same subspace of $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$.
2. There are constants $0<c_k\le C_k<\infty$, depending only on $n$ and $k$,
   with
$$c_k^{1/2}\,\|\langle\xi\rangle^k\mathcal F_2f\|_2\le\|f\|_{W^{k,2}} \le C_k^{1/2}\,\|\langle\xi\rangle^k\mathcal F_2f\|_2,$$
   and $\|\langle\xi\rangle^k\mathcal F_2f\|_2=\|\Phi(f)\|_{H^k}$. Hence the
   weak-derivative norm and the bracket-weighted $L^2$ norm are equivalent,
   and the latter is also equivalent to
   $\|(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{k/2}\mathcal F_2f\|_2$, by
$$\|\langle\xi\rangle^k h\|_2\le\|(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{k/2}h\|_2 \le(2\pi)^k\|\langle\xi\rangle^k h\|_2,\qquad h\in L^2 .$$
3. The three norm expressions are **not** identical in general: the
   bracket-weighted norm differs from both the weak-derivative norm and the
   Laplacian-weighted norm, as the Gaussian computation in the proof shows.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ be the Sobolev space of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]] with the weak gradient $\nabla u$ of
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]], write
$r(x):=|x|$, and write $\|u\|_2^2=\int_{\mathbb R^3}|u(x)|^2\,dx$ for the
$L^2$ norm of [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Then:

(a) for every $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\};\mathbb C)$,

$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{|u(x)|^2}{|x|^2}\,dx\le 4\int_{\mathbb R^3}|\nabla u(x)|^2\,dx;$$

(b) the same inequality holds for every $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$;

(c) for every $u\in W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ the a.e.-defined function $x\mapsto u(x)/|x|$ lies in $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ and satisfies $\|u/|\cdot|\|_2\le 2\|\nabla u\|_2$.

No constant smaller than $4$ is claimed, and no statement is made about
$\|u/|\cdot|\|_2$ for $u$ outside $W^{1,2}$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p<\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then the compactly supported smooth
functions $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ are dense in
$W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$: for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ with
$$\|\varphi-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)}<\delta.$$
No such norm-density assertion is made for $p=\infty$.

Let a finite gluing of elementary solid regions be given, with union $E$ and outer boundary presentation $\Sigma^{\mathrm{out}}=\bigl((D_1,\varphi_1),\ldots,(D_M,\varphi_M)\bigr)$. Vector-valued integrals below are taken coordinatewise, so that for a continuous $\mathbb R^3$-valued $W$ on $E$ the symbol $\iiint_EW$ denotes the vector whose $k$th coordinate is $\int_EW_k$, and for a continuous $\mathbb R^3$-valued $Z$ on the boundary the symbol $\iint_{\partial E}Z$ denotes the vector whose $k$th coordinate is $\sum_{j=1}^M\int_{D_j}Z_k(\varphi_j)$, where $n$ inside such an integrand is read as the oriented area vector $\varphi_{j,u}\times\varphi_{j,v}$ of the patch, exactly as in the scalar flux.

Then, for $f$ of class $C^1$ on an open set containing $E$ and $F$ of class $C^1$ on an open set containing $E$,

$$\iiint_E\nabla f=\iint_{\partial E}fn,\qquad \iiint_E\operatorname{curl}F=\iint_{\partial E}n\times F.$$

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T$ be a densely defined linear operator on $H$.

- $T$ is **symmetric** when $T\subseteq T^*$, that is, $D(T)\subseteq D(T^*)$ and
  $Tx=T^*x$ for all $x\in D(T)$; equivalently
  $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,Ty\rangle$ for all $x,y\in D(T)$.
- $T$ is **self-adjoint** when $T=T^*$, that is, the domains and the values
  agree.
- $T$ is **essentially self-adjoint** when its closure $\overline T$ is
  self-adjoint; by [[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]] this presupposes
  that $T$ is closable.

**Consequences, with proofs.** These are part of the content of the definition.

1. *A symmetric $T$ is closable.* $T\subseteq T^*$ and $T^*$ is closed
   ([[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]]), so $T^*$ is a closed
   extension of $T$. In particular the closure $\overline T$ exists and
   $\overline T\subseteq T^*$.
2. *The closure of a symmetric operator is symmetric.* If $T\subseteq T^*$,
   the inclusion reversal of
   [[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]] applied to
   $T\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq T^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$. Applying it once more to the inclusion
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq(T^{**})^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^{***}$. Since $\overline T=T^{**}$ and
   $(\overline T)^*=T^{***}$
   ([[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]]), this reads
   $\overline T\subseteq(\overline T)^*$: the closure is symmetric. (Each
   application is legitimate because the adjoint is defined once its operator
   is densely defined, and $D(T^{**})$ is dense because
   $T\subseteq T^{**}=\overline T$, so that $D(T^{**})$ contains the dense
   domain $D(T)$.)
3. *A self-adjoint operator has no proper symmetric extension.* If $T=T^*$ and
   $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*$, then $S^*\subseteq T^*$ by inclusion reversal,
   so $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*\subseteq T^*=T$ and all inclusions are
   equalities.
4. *A self-adjoint operator is closed*, being equal to the adjoint $T^*$ of the
   densely defined $T$, and *an essentially self-adjoint operator has exactly
   one self-adjoint extension*, namely $\overline T$: a self-adjoint extension
   $S$ of $T$ is closed, hence contains the least closed extension
   $\overline T$, and then $S\subseteq S^*\subseteq(\overline T)^*=\overline T$
   by item 2 and symmetry, so $S=\overline T$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $T$ be a
densely defined linear operator on $H$, with domain $D(T)$ dense in $H$
([[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]], [[def-dense-top]]).
Since $D(T)$ is dense, and since $H$ is complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]), every
bounded linear functional on the normed space $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]) extends uniquely to a bounded linear
functional $\widetilde\varphi$ on $H$ of the same norm, by setting
$\widetilde\varphi(z)=\lim_n\varphi(z_n)$ for any sequence $z_n\in D(T)$ with
$z_n\to z$ in $H$; the limit exists because $\varphi$ is bounded on a dense
subspace and $H$ is complete, and it does not depend on the sequence because a
bounded functional is uniformly continuous.

A vector $y\in H$ belongs to the **adjoint domain** $D(T^*)$ when the linear
functional $\varphi_y:D(T)\to\mathbb C$, $\varphi_y(x)=\langle Tx,y\rangle$, is
bounded on $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$. In that case Hilbert space Riesz representation
([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) applied to the extension
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$ produces a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with
$$T^*y\text{ is the unique }w\in H\text{ such that }\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,w\rangle\quad\text{for all }x\in D(T),$$
equivalently $\widetilde{\varphi_y}(z)=\langle z,T^*y\rangle$ for all $z\in H$.
The map $T^*:D(T^*)\to H$, $y\mapsto T^*y$, is the **adjoint** of $T$.

**Well-definedness.** The functional $\varphi_y$ is linear in $x$ for each
$y$, so its domain of boundedness $D(T^*)$ is a linear subspace: if
$\varphi_y,\varphi_{y'}$ are bounded so is $\varphi_{ay+by'}$ for scalars
$a,b$, because the first-variable-linear convention gives
$\varphi_{ay+by'}=\overline a\,\varphi_y+\overline b\,\varphi_{y'}$. On
$D(T^*)$ the map $T^*$ is linear: if $y,y'$ are represented by $w,w'$, then
$ay+by'$ is represented by $aw+bw'$, since
$\langle x,aw+bw'\rangle=\overline a\langle x,w\rangle+
\overline b\langle x,w'\rangle$; the representing vector is unique. By Riesz representation for the Hilbert space
$H$ a vector $w\in H$ is determined by the values $\langle z,w\rangle$ with
$z$ ranging over $H$, and those values are determined by the functional
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$. Equivalently, if $w,w'$ both represent $\varphi_y$,
then $\langle x,w-w'\rangle=0$ for every $x\in D(T)$; density of $D(T)$ and
continuity of the inner product extend this equality to every $x\in H$, and
taking $x=w-w'$ gives $w=w'$. Finally only
ambient-norm boundedness of $\varphi_y$ on $D(T)$ is required: no extension,
no closure and no closedness of $T$ is presupposed.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$. Then every $x\in H$ has a unique decomposition

$$x=m+n,\qquad m\in M,\quad n\in M^\perp ,$$

so that $H=M\oplus M^\perp$ as a direct sum of the subspace $M$ and its orthogonal complement.

derivations.claim: [Normalization] By polar coordinates and [F2], $\|\psi_{100}\|_2^2=N^2 4\pi\int_0^\infty r^2e^{-2\alpha r}dr=(\gamma^3/2)2/\gamma^3=1$.

[Free maximal realization without arbitrary choice] For the real multiplier $t(\xi)=4\pi^2|\xi|^2$, truncate any $g\in L^2$ to $g_n=\mathbf1_{\{t\le n\}}g$ to prove density of $D(M_t)$. It is symmetric because $t$ is real. If $g\in D(M_t^*)$ with adjoint value $h$, testing against every $L^2$ function supported in $\{t\le n\}$ gives $h=tg$ there. These sets increase to all space, so $tg=h\in L^2$ and $D(M_t^*)=D(M_t)$. Thus $M_t$ and its unitary conjugate $T$ are self-adjoint, with $D(T)=H^2$ by [F3]. For $z\notin\mathbb R$, $R_0(z)=\mathcal F_2^*M_{(t-z)^{-1}}\mathcal F_2$ is the actual two-sided inverse, since $t/(t-z)$ is bounded and $(T-z)R_0(z)=I$, $R_0(z)(T-z)=I$ on $D(T)$.

[Hardy relative bound and Neumann realization] Put $Bu=-\gamma u/r$ for $u\in H^2$. By [F3] and Fourier Cauchy–Schwarz, $\|Bu\|_2\le2\gamma\|\nabla u\|_2\le2\gamma\|Tu\|_2^{1/2}\|u\|_2^{1/2}\le\varepsilon\|Tu\|_2+\gamma^2\varepsilon^{-1}\|u\|_2$ for every $\varepsilon>0$. Choose $Y>16\gamma^2$ and $\varepsilon=1/4$. The exact free multipliers give $\|TR_0(\pm iY)\|\le1$, $\|R_0(\pm iY)\|\le1/Y$, and hence $\|BR_0(\pm iY)\|<1/2$. The operator series $\sum_{j\ge0}(-BR_0(\pm iY))^j$ converges in norm, and $R_0(\pm iY)(I+BR_0(\pm iY))^{-1}$ maps into $D(T)$ and is the two-sided inverse of $C\mp iY$ for $C=T+B$ on $H^2$. This proves surjectivity of both nonreal signs with the exact factor order.

[Radial law and moments] By [F1], $p(r)=r^2\int_{S^2}|\psi_{100}(r\Omega)|^2d\sigma=4a_0^{-3}r^2e^{-2r/a_0}$. By [F2], its integral is $4a_0^{-3}2/(2/a_0)^3=1$ and its first moment is $4a_0^{-3}6/(2/a_0)^4=3a_0/2$.

[Exact adjoint domain] $C$ is densely defined and symmetric because both $T$ and the real multiplication $B$ are symmetric on $H^2$. Let $y\in D(C^*)$, fix $z=iY$, and let $x=(C-z)^{-1}(C^*-z)y\in D(C)$. Then $(C^*-z)(y-x)=0$. Since $\operatorname{ran}(C-\overline z)=L^2$, adjoint pairing shows $\ker(C^*-z)=\{0\}$; consequently $y=x\in D(C)$. Thus $D(C^*)=D(C)=H^2$ and $C=C^*$, not merely a formally symmetric differential expression. All constructions are explicit sequences/truncations or single-vector existential arguments under CC.

[Weak $H^2$ domain of the actual exponential] On $r>0$ let $f=e^{-\alpha r}$ and $\Omega_i=x_i/r$. Its classical derivatives are $\partial_i f=-\alpha f\Omega_i$ and $\partial_j\partial_i f=\alpha^2 f\Omega_i\Omega_j-\alpha f(\delta_{ij}-\Omega_i\Omega_j)/r$. Each is in $L^2(\mathbb R^3)$: the first derivatives are bounded times an exponential and second derivatives are bounded by $2\alpha^2f+2\alpha f/r$, with $\int_0^1 r^2/r^2\,dr<\infty$ and exponential tails. These are also the weak derivatives on all space. Indeed, integrate against a compactly supported smooth test function over $r>\delta$ and let $\delta\downarrow0$; each inner-sphere boundary term has magnitude bounded by a constant times its area $4\pi\delta^2$, because $f$ and its first derivatives are bounded. It tends to zero, and the volume integrals converge since the displayed derivatives are locally integrable. Thus no origin-supported delta term is present and $f\in H^2$, even though it is not classically differentiable at zero. Summing the weak second derivatives gives $-\Delta f=(-\alpha^2+2\alpha/r)f$ almost everywhere; hence $Cf=-\alpha^2 f$ because $\gamma=2\alpha$. Multiplication by $N$ preserves the domain and gives the claimed eigenvalue $-\gamma^2/4$.

[The level is the ground level, locally] For a compactly supported smooth $v$, integrate $\operatorname{div}\Omega=2/r$ on punctured balls; the inner flux of $|v|^2\Omega$ is $O(\delta^2)$ and vanishes. Expanding the square gives $\|
abla v+\alpha\Omega v\|_2^2=\|
abla v\|_2^2+\alpha^2\|v\|_2^2-2\alpha\int |v|^2/r$. By $H^1$ smooth density and the Hardy inequality, all these terms extend continuously to $H^1$: for example $\int |v|^2/r\le\|v/r\|_2\|v\|_2$. For $v\in D(C)=H^2$, Fourier pairing then gives $\langle Cv,vangle+\alpha^2\|v\|_2^2=\|
abla v+\alpha\Omega v\|_2^2\ge0$. Thus $C\ge-\alpha^2$. For any real $\lambda<-\alpha^2$, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\|(C-\lambda)v\|_2\ge(-\alpha^2-\lambda)\|v\|_2$; self-adjointness makes its range closed, and the orthogonal complement of the range is $\ker(C-\lambda)=\{0\}$, so its range is all $L^2$ and its inverse is bounded. Such $\lambda$ is outside the spectrum. Step 4.1 supplies an eigenvector at the lower bound, so this is a ground vector. No negative-spectrum theorem or AC spectral calculus is needed.

[Degree-zero Laguerre identity without Kummer dependence] The degree-zero generalized Laguerre polynomial is $L_0^{(a)}(s)=1$: equivalently the degree-zero normalized solution of $sv''+(a+1-s)v'=0$ is $v\equiv1$. In the reduced $l=0$ equation $-u''-\gamma u/r=-\alpha^2u$, substitution $u=r e^{-\alpha r}v(2\alpha r)$ produces $s v''+(2-s)v'=0$ since $\gamma=2\alpha$. Its degree-zero normalized solution $L_0^{(1)}=1$ therefore gives exactly $u=r e^{-\alpha r}$. Normalization supplies $u_{10}=2a_0^{-3/2}r e^{-r/a_0}$ and $\psi_{100}=u_{10}Y_{00}/r$ with the same constant as step 1.1. This is the claimed special polynomial-exponential case; it does not invoke a general radial completeness theorem.

[Conclusion] Steps 1.1, 4.1, 2.2 and 5.2 prove (a)–(d), and steps 1.2, 2.1 and 3.1 prove its exact self-adjoint realization, step 4.1 proves the weak ground-vector domain, and step 5.1 proves the ground lower bound under CC alone.
